with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
columns = list(rows[0])

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="International Health Survey 2024", agency="health-research.example.org"
)
# RespondentID is assigned, not asked, so it gets no question.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Country": "In which country do you live?",
    "Age": "How old are you?",
    "Sex": "What is your sex?",
    "HeightCm": "How tall are you, in centimetres?",
    "WeightKg": "How much do you weigh, in kilograms?",
    "SmokingStatus": "Which of these best describes your smoking?",
    "ExerciseFrequency": "How often do you exercise for at least 30 minutes?",
    "AlcoholDrinksPerWeek": "How many alcoholic drinks do you have in a typical week?",
    "SelfRatedHealth": "In general, how would you rate your health?",
    "ChronicCondition": "Do you have a long-term health condition?",
    "DoctorVisitsLastYear": "How many times did you see a doctor in the last 12 months?",
    "HasHealthInsurance": "Do you have health insurance?",
    "SleepHours": "On a typical night, how many hours do you sleep?",
    "Wellbeing": "On a scale of 0 to 10, how satisfied are you with your life?",
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}

for col in ("SmokingStatus", "ExerciseFrequency"):
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col} Codes")
    add_codes(doc, code_list, sorted({row[col] for row in rows}))
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

for name in (
    "Physical Health",
    "Mental Health",
    "Access to Healthcare",
    "Demographics",
):
    doc.add_concept(name=name)
doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18 and over in the participating countries")

# Lineage: BMI is computed from height and weight
bmi = doc.add_variable(name="BMI", label="Body mass index")

# Linkage: the register is a second study, joined on RespondentID
register = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2024")

link = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-register linkage 2024")

)
link.add_variable_map(
    variables["RespondentID"].to_reference(),
    register_key.to_reference(),
    correspondence=exact,
)
link.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")
linked = doc.add_variable(name="HealthByHospitalUse")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    variables["SelfRatedHealth"].to_reference(),

]

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]

# -> v1: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("health-survey-v1.xml")

# Version 2

    text="How many times did you see a dentist in the last 12 months?"
)
doc.add_variable(name="DentistVisitsLastYear", question=dentist)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(

study.version_responsibility = "Principal Investigator"
print(f"v2: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors")

Track C: Archivist: Enrich and Version Existing DDI Files: Sample solution

One loop over the three files from step 1.

from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

ARCHIVE_FIELDS = {
    "archive:accession_date": "Date the archive received the file.",
    "archive:depositor": "Team that deposited the file.",
    "archive:retention": "How long the archive keeps the file.",
    "archive:access": "Who may use the data: open, registered or restricted.",
}
YES_NO_FILES = {3}  # from the plan: study 3 asks a yes/no question


def set_archive_field(item, key, value):
    if key not in ARCHIVE_FIELDS:
        raise KeyError(f"{key!r} is not in the archive catalog")
    item.set_property(key, value)


def count_archive_fields(doc):
    items = [doc.study_unit, *doc.questions, *doc.variables]
    return sum(
        any(key.startswith("archive:") for key in item.properties) for item in items
    )


for i in (1, 2, 3):
    doc = ddi.open_ddi(f"study-{i}.xml")
    if not doc.concepts:
        doc.add_concept(name="Social Sciences")
    if not doc.universes:
        doc.add_universe(name="General population")
    variable, question = doc.variables[0], doc.questions[0]
    if not variable.question_references:
        variable.question_references = [question.to_reference()]
    if i in YES_NO_FILES:
        yes_no = doc.add_code_list(name="Yes/No")
        for value, label in (("1", "Yes"), ("2", "No")):
            category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
            yes_no.codes.append(
                CodeItem(
                    agency=yes_no.agency,
                    identifier=str(uuid4()),
                    version=yes_no.version,
                    value=value,
                    category=category.to_reference(),
                )
            )
        variable.set_coded(yes_no)

    study = doc.study_unit
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:accession_date", "2024-11-04")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:depositor", f"Research team {i}")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:retention", "permanent")
    set_archive_field(variable, "archive:access", "open")

    study.increment_version()
    study.version_rationales.append(
        VersionRationale(
            descriptions=[
                InternationalString(
                    text="Enriched metadata: added concept, universe, question link and archive fields"
                )
            ]
        )
    )
    study.version_responsibility = "Archive Metadata Team"

    lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
    print(
        f"study-{i}: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, "
        f"{len(lint_errors)} lint errors, "
        f"{count_archive_fields(doc)} items with archive fields"
    )
    doc.save(f"study-{i}-enriched.xml")
# -> study-3: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors, 2 items with archive fields

Track D: NSO Staff: Build a Census Instrument: Sample solution

One complete script, using census-data.csv. Run validate.sh (or validate.ps1) from step 11 after it.

import csv
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    IfThenElse,
    Instrument,
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
)
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem
from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, load_spec


def add_codes(doc, code_list, labels):
    """Add one Category and one Code per label, numbered from 1."""
    for number, label in enumerate(labels, start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )


def rationale(text):
    return VersionRationale(descriptions=[InternationalString(text=text)])


with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
columns = list(rows[0])

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census 2024", agency="ca.statcan")
# HouseholdID and PersonNumber are assigned, not asked.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Province": "In which province or territory do you live?",
    "Age": "What was your age at your last birthday?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "MaritalStatus": "What is your marital status?",
    "RelationshipToHead": "What is your relationship to Person 1?",
    "CountryOfBirth": "In which country were you born?",
    "Citizenship": "Of what country are you a citizen?",
    "MotherTongue": "What language did you first learn at home in childhood?",
    "HighestEducation": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
    "EmploymentType": "Last week, were you an employee, self-employed, or not working?",
    "Occupation": "What was your main kind of work last week?",
    "WeeklyHoursWorked": "How many hours did you work last week?",
    "AnnualIncome": "What was your total income last year?",
    "CommuteMode": "How did you usually get to work last week?",
    "HousingType": "What type of dwelling do you live in?",
    "Tenure": "Is this dwelling owned or rented by a member of this household?",
    "Rooms": "How many rooms are in this dwelling?",
    "YearBuilt": "In what year was this dwelling built?",
    "HouseholdSize": "How many people usually live here?",
    "InternetAccess": "Does this household have access to the internet at home?",
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}

for col in ("Province", "Gender", "MaritalStatus", "EmploymentType", "HousingType"):
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col}Codes")
    add_codes(doc, code_list, sorted({row[col] for row in rows}))
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

doc.add_concept(name="Population")
doc.add_concept(name="Labour")
doc.add_universe(name="All persons usually resident in private dwellings")
variables["Occupation"].set_property("classification", "ISCO-08")
variables["AnnualIncome"].set_property("referencePeriod", "Calendar year 2023")

# The flow: everyone answers the person section; the labour section has a gate
AGE_GATE = "Age >= 15"


def ask(col):
    return doc.add_item(
        QuestionConstruct, name=col, question_reference=questions[col].to_reference()
    )


person = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="person",
    control_construct_references=[ask(c).to_reference() for c in ("Age", "Gender")],
)
labour = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="labour",
    control_construct_references=[
        ask(c).to_reference()
        for c in ("EmploymentType", "Occupation", "WeeklyHoursWorked")
    ],
)
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Working-age gate")
gate.set_condition(AGE_GATE, description="Persons aged 15 and over")
gate.then_construct_reference = labour.to_reference()
main = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Census flow",
    control_construct_references=[person.to_reference(), gate.to_reference()],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Census 2024 questionnaire")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main.to_reference()

# The spec of the same flow. A person with no age skips the labour section.
Path("census.spec.yaml").write_text(
    """\
spec: census-2024
version: "1"
modules:
  - id: person
    questions:
      - id: Age
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 120, decimals: 0}}
  - id: labour
    gate: Age >= 15
    questions:
      - id: EmploymentType
        domain: {text: {max_length: 40}}
      - id: Occupation
        domain: {text: {max_length: 60}}
      - id: WeeklyHoursWorked
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 168, decimals: 0}}
""",
    encoding="utf-8",
)
spec = load_spec("census.spec.yaml")
print(f"Gates agree: {equivalent(spec.module('labour').gate_text, AGE_GATE)}")
# -> Gates agree: True

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v1: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
doc.save("census-v1.xml")

# Version 2: one question added
q_internet = doc.add_question(text="Do you have access to high-speed internet?")
doc.add_variable(name="HighSpeedInternet", question=q_internet)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(rationale("Added internet access question"))
study.version_responsibility = "Census Content Team"
doc.save("census-v2.xml")

# Version 3: five questions added, three retired with their variables
for text in [
    "What is your primary language at home?",
    "Do you identify as Indigenous?",
    "What is your highest degree?",
    "Do you have a disability?",
    "What is your annual household income?",
]:
    doc.add_question(text=text)
for col in ("Province", "MaritalStatus", "HousingType"):
    doc.remove(variables[col].identifier)
    doc.remove(questions[col].identifier)
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales = [
    rationale("Major redesign: added equity and income questions")
]

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v2: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
# -> v2: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("census-v3.xml")

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
Exercise 1

pairs = [
    ("missing(PetKind)", "empty(PetKind) or refused(PetKind)"),
    ("PetAge > 10", "PetAge * 2 > 20"),
    ("PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 2", "PetKind != 3"),
    ('PetName = "Rex"', 'PetName < "S"'),
]
for left, right in pairs:
    verdict = decide(left, right, types=types)
    if verdict.outcome == "different":
        print(f"different: {verdict.example.describe()}")
    elif verdict.outcome == "unknown":
        print(f"unknown: {verdict.reason}")
    else:
        print(verdict.outcome)

(a) is the definition of missing(). (b) is arithmetic. (c) differs for a code that neither gate names: the solver does not read the Species list, so for it a fourth code exists. A respondent with two codes, 1 and 3, also tells them apart. (d) compares text by order, which the solver does not model.

Exercise 2

print(decide("PetAge > 30", "PetAge >= 31").example.describe())  # -> PetAge is 30.25
print(decide("PetAge > 30", "PetAge >= 31", types=types).outcome)  # -> equivalent

Without types, a pet can be 30.25 years old, which PetAge > 30 accepts and PetAge >= 31 does not. The spec gives PetAge decimals: 0, so spec_types() makes it an integer, and no whole number lies between 30 and 31.

Exercise 3

aged_31 = {"PetAge": Answer("answered", frozenset({Fraction(31)}))}
everyone = [*respondents.values(), aged_31]
print([evaluate("PetAge > 30", answers) for answers in everyone])
print([evaluate("missing(PetAge)", answers) for answers in everyone])
dont_know = "answered(PetAge) and not (PetAge > 30 or PetAge <= 30)"
print([evaluate(dont_know, answers) for answers in everyone])

The "did not know" respondent is caught by neither: the answer has no value, so the comparison is false, and it is answered, so it is not missing. The expressions have no word for "don't know", but the third edit says it: the age is answered, yet neither PetAge > 30 nor PetAge <= 30 holds, which happens only when there is no value to compare.

Exercise 4

housing = {"Own": "code", "YearsOwned": "integer"}
for question, gate in intended.items():
    verdict = decide(gate, translated[question], types=housing)
    if verdict.outcome == "different":
        print(f"{question}: differs when {verdict.example.describe()}")
    else:
        print(f"{question}: {verdict.outcome}")

Mortgage is the one to raise. With Own = 1, a respondent who answers "don't know" to Own, or leaves it empty or refuses it, skips the mortgage question but still sees YearsOwned. Either both questions use not Own = 2, or the survey owner decides they are for home owners only and both use Own = 1. The two gates written differently for Refinanced agree for every whole number of years.

Exercise 5

verdict = decide("not PetAge > 10", "PetAge <= 10", types=types)
print(evaluate("not PetAge > 10", verdict.example.answers))  # -> True
print(evaluate("PetAge <= 10", verdict.example.answers))  # -> False

Whatever respondent the solver gives (an empty, refused or "don't know" age), one gate holds and the other does not. ddi-l makes the same check on every different verdict before it reports one.

Exercise 6

(a) A household with exactly one pet skips the pets module, though the spec asks it about its pet. The spec is the record, so fix the instrument's gate, unless the survey owner says that one-pet households were meant to skip it; then fix the spec and give it a new version.

(b) With the extra, nothing: the spec says PetCount is a whole number, and for whole numbers PetCount >= 1 and PetCount > 0 agree. Without it, spec.gate.different, because the normal forms differ. That finding is a false alarm, which is why the report shows both normal forms.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): decide() returns different. What do you know?

B. A different verdict comes with one respondent the gates disagree on. A is true but says less: gates written differently can still be equivalent. C and D do not follow.

Question 2 (O3): A respondent answers PetAge with “don't know”. Is missing(PetAge) true?

B. missing(x) is empty(x) or refused(x). An answer without a value is neither, and any comparison of it is false.

Question 3 (O2): Why does decide() say PetCount > 0 and PetCount >= 1 differ, until you pass types?

B. types={"PetCount": "integer"}, which spec_types() reads from decimals: 0, rules out fractions, and the two agree.

Question 4 (O1): decide() returns unknown. What do you do?

C. unknown means the solver could not decide, for the reason given. The verdict is the same on every run, so D does not help.

Question 5 (O5): Without the logic extra, ddi conform reports spec.gate.different for a gate. What can you conclude?

B. Without the extra nothing is calculated: PetCount >= 1 against PetCount > 0 is reported, though no household is routed differently.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
Exercise 1

print(client.get("/v1/versions").json())
openapi = client.get("/schema/openapi.json").json()
lint = openapi["paths"]["/v1/lint"]["post"]
print([parameter["name"] for parameter in lint["parameters"]])

/v1/versions lists the DDI versions the service validates against, and the one it uses when a document does not say. The OpenAPI document is what the interactive documentation is drawn from, so its list matches what you found in the browser.

Exercise 2

config = '{"allowed_agencies": ["ca.statcan"]}'
found = client.post("/v1/lint", params={"lint_config": config}, content=xml)
print([finding["rule_id"] for finding in found.json()["lint_findings"]])
checked = client.post("/v1/validate", params={"lint_config": config}, content=xml)
print(checked.json()["valid"])

ddi.agency.allowed reports the agency example.org, which the list does not allow. It is a warning, like the two missing labels, so the document is still valid. The configuration applies to this request only: the next request without it gets the default checks.

Exercise 3

broken = xml.replace(b"<r:Version>1</r:Version>", b"<r:Version>one</r:Version>", 1)
answer = client.post("/v1/validate", content=broken)
report = answer.json()
print(answer.status_code, report["valid"])
issue = report["schema_issues"][0]
print(issue["line"], issue["message"])

The status code is 200: the service read the document and did its job. The document is what is wrong, so valid is false and the error says where.

Exercise 4

as_json = client.post("/v1/convert/json", content=xml)
back = client.post(
    "/v1/convert/xml",
    content=as_json.content,
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
)
print(back.content == xml)

The JSON keeps everything the XML holds, so the round trip is exact. Its keys carry each element's namespace in braces, as in ddi to-json: look at as_json.json() to see them.

Exercise 5

(a) /v1/validate takes a document, so it needs POST with the document as the body. (b) The service knows DDI 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 (see /v1/versions): drop version or pick one of those. (c) The default limit is 32 MB: whoever runs the service raises it, for example ddi serve --max-body-mb 64. (d) The service is working on as many documents as it may: wait the seconds in Retry-After and send it again. A client written for a service should do this on its own.

Exercise 6

from ddi_l.server import ServerConfig

deposit = create_app(
    ServerConfig(
        max_body_bytes=100 * 1024 * 1024,
        cors_allow_origins=("https://deposit.example.org",),
        enable_openapi=False,
    )
)
checker = TestClient(app=deposit)
print(checker.get("/schema").status_code)
preflight = checker.options(
    "/v1/validate",
    headers={
        "Origin": "https://deposit.example.org",
        "Access-Control-Request-Method": "POST",
    },
)
print(preflight.headers["access-control-allow-origin"])

A browser asks the service first (this OPTIONS request is the "preflight") and sends the deposit only when the answer names the form's site. The command with the same settings:

ddi serve --host 0.0.0.0 --max-body-mb 100 --cors-allow-origin https://deposit.example.org --no-openapi

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): You start ddi serve on your laptop. A colleague on another machine cannot reach it. Why?

B. The default keeps a service you are trying out private to your machine.

Question 2 (O2): /v1/validate answers 200 with valid false. What does it mean?

C. 200 says the request worked. valid is about the document, and only errors make it false.

Question 3 (O4): Which status code says that the service could not read the body at all?

B. 400 Bad Request: not XML, not JSON, or a parameter it does not know. 413 means the body was too large to read.

Question 4 (O3): Which header do you send with a JSON body to /v1/convert/xml?

B. Content-Type says what the body is. Without it, the service cannot tell JSON from anything else.

Question 5 (O5): A web page on the site forms.example.org must call the service from the browser. What do you set?

A. Name each site that may call the service. There is no wildcard, so that a deployment never opens to every site by mistake.

items.title: Module 20 (optional): From DDI-Codebook to DDI-Lifecycle, built for reuse
Exercises
items.text:
Exercise 1

Each file gets its own PetKind question and its own code list, with different URNs: nothing says that 2022 and 2023 asked the same question with the same categories, which is exactly what comparing the waves needs. A corrected category label has to be corrected in every file again. Converting all waves together, and writing each repeated item once, keeps that knowledge in the metadata.

Exercise 2

source = Path("pets-2023.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
source = source.replace(
    'xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_5" version="2.5"',
    'xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_6" version="2.6"',
)
source = source.replace(
    "    <dataAccs>\n",
    "    <dataAccs>\n"
    '      <license URI="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">'
    "CC BY 4.0</license>\n",
)
Path("pets-2023-2.6.xml").write_text(source, encoding="utf-8")

root_26 = ET.parse("pets-2023-2.6.xml").getroot()
C_26 = {"c": root_26.tag[1:].split("}")[0]}
licence = root_26.find("c:stdyDscr/c:dataAccs/c:license", C_26)
print(C_26["c"], licence.get("URI"))
# -> ddi:codebook:2_6 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

read_codebook() reads this file as it is, because it takes the namespace from the root. A converter can take the licence from license/@URI when a codebook has one, and ask a person when it has only useStmt text.

Exercise 3

write_codebook(
    2024,
    "10.5072/FK2PETS24",
    "How many pets live in your household?",
    ["PetCount", "PetKind", "SecondPetKind"],
)
waves[2024] = read_codebook("pets-2024.xml")
questions, code_lists, universes = repeats(waves)
print(len(questions), len(code_lists))  # -> 4 1
tables = build_tables(waves)
print(len(tables["questions"]), len(tables["variables"]))  # -> 4 8

The third wave adds a study, a data file and three variables, and not one question or code list: its variables refer to the items the first two waves already have.

Exercise 4

same = {"How many pets live in your household?": "How many pets live in your home?"}
for wave in waves.values():
    for var in wave["variables"]:
        var["question"] = same.get(var["question"], var["question"])
tables = build_tables(waves)
print(len(tables["questions"]))  # -> 3
write_tables("pets-tables", tables)
loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
first = loaded.get("variables", "PetCount_2022").question_references[0]
last = loaded.get("variables", "PetCount_2024").question_references[0]
print(first.urn == last.urn)  # -> True

The decision is recorded in one place, the same mapping, which the owner can review. The question keeps the 2022 wording; if the 2023 wording should be kept as well, a new version of the question (Module 15) records the change instead.

Exercise 5

french = {
    "PetCount": "Nombre d'animaux",
    "PetKind": "Type d'animal",
    "SecondPetKind": "Type du deuxième animal",
}
for variable in tables["variables"]:
    variable["label@fr"] = french[variable["name"]]
for question in tables["questions"]:
    asker = next(v for v in tables["variables"] if v["question"] == question["id"])
    question["label@en"] = asker["label@en"]
    question["label@fr"] = french[asker["name"]]
write_tables("pets-tables", tables)

loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
labels = loaded.get("variables", "PetKind_2023").labels
print(next(label.text for label in labels if label.lang == "fr"))
# -> Type d'animal
print(len(run_lint(loaded.to_fragment())))  # -> 0

The column header carries the language, so label@en and label@fr become one label with two strings. Because each question is written once, it is translated once, for every wave.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): Why can two DDI-Codebook files not share PetKind's categories?

B. Each wave's codebook writes the categories again. In DDI-Lifecycle the code list is an item with a URN, which every wave's variables refer to.

Question 2 (O3): The 2022 and 2023 codebooks word one question differently. What does the converter of this module do?

B. A variable name is not a question. A program can compare wordings, but whether two wordings ask the same thing is a decision.

Question 3 (O4): In the tables, what ties PetKind_2023 to the 2023 study?

B. The question is shared by both waves; the data file belongs to one study, and the variable is a column of that file.

Question 4 (O4): Two waves, three variables with the same four categories. How many code lists does the DDI-Lifecycle file hold?

B. The categories are compared as a whole, and the same set becomes one code list.

Question 5 (O5): A codebook's conditions of use say “Free to reuse with attribution (CC BY 4.0).” What should the converted file hold?

B. A web address names one licence without ambiguity, and a program can recognize it. The sentence is clear to a person only.

items.title: Module 21 (optional): Describe your data with DDI-CDI
Exercises
items.text:
Exercise 1

(a) DDI-Codebook, or DDI-Lifecycle if the archive wants item-level reuse: one study and its file. (b) DDI-Lifecycle: each question and code list is an item with its own identifier and version, referred to by every wave. (c) DDI-CDI: data from different domains and shapes, and the processes that link them. The survey's questionnaire would still be described in DDI-Lifecycle.

Exercise 2

written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for variable in written.iterfind("cdi:InstanceVariable", N):
    name = variable.findtext("cdi:name/cdi:name", namespaces=N)
    domains = [
        valid_type.text for valid_type in variable.iterfind("*/cdi:validType", N)
    ]
    print(name, domains)

A link holds the class of the object it points to in validType, so a program knows what it will find without following the link. HouseholdId and PetCount have no code list, so this sketch gives them no value domain.

Exercise 3

A long data structure (LongDataStructure). HouseholdId is an identifier component, as in the wide file. Variable is a variable descriptor component: its values name the variables, and it is defined by a descriptor variable whose values are PetKind and PetCount. Value is a variable value component: it holds the values of several variables in one column. PetKind and PetCount keep their instance variables and value domains.

Exercise 4

def label(*strings):
    """A label in each language given, as (text, language) pairs."""
    return cdi(
        "displayLabel",
        *(
            cdi(
                "languageSpecificString",
                cdi("content", text=text),
                cdi("language", text=language),
            )
            for text, language in strings
        ),
    )


french = {"Dog": "Chien", "Cat": "Chat", "Other pet": "Autre animal"}
french["Don't know"] = "Ne sait pas"
written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for category in written.iterfind("cdi:Category", N):
    english = category.findtext(
        "cdi:displayLabel/cdi:languageSpecificString/cdi:content", namespaces=N
    )
    category.remove(category.find("cdi:displayLabel", N))
    category.insert(0, label((english, "en"), (french[english], "fr")))
ET.indent(written)
ET.ElementTree(written).write("pets-cdi.xml", encoding="utf-8", xml_declaration=True)
print(
    sum(1 for language in written.iter(f"{{{CDI}}}language") if language.text == "fr")
)  # -> 4

The new label goes first in each category, where the schema puts displayLabel, before identifier. Validate the file again to check.

Exercise 5

pet_kind = tables.get("variables", "PetKind")
print(pet_kind.to_reference().urn)
# -> urn:ddi:example.org:e96e0842-d74e-5893-a7ba-b3c3fabda24d:1
written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for variable in written.iterfind("cdi:InstanceVariable", N):
    if variable.findtext("cdi:name/cdi:name", namespaces=N) == "PetKind":
        parts = variable.find("cdi:identifier/cdi:ddiIdentifier", N)
        print([part.text for part in parts])
# -> ['variable-PetKind', 'example.org', '1']

Both have an agency, an identifier and a version. The DDI-CDI file uses identifiers of its own, such as variable-PetKind. To make the two descriptions of the variable the same object, give DDI-CDI the DDI-Lifecycle identifier: pass pet_kind.identifier and pet_kind.version to identifier() instead.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does DDI-CDI describe that DDI-Lifecycle does not?

B. Questionnaires are DDI-Lifecycle's strength; both have code lists. DDI-CDI describes data in any shape, from any domain, down to a single value.

Question 2 (O2): A variable has the codes 1 Dog, 2 Cat and 9 Don't know. How does DDI-CDI hold them?

B. DDI-CDI separates the answers from the values that stand for something else. DDI-Lifecycle does it with one code list and the isMissing flag of a category.

Question 3 (O3): In a wide data structure, what does the household identifier column get?

B. Identifier components tell the rows apart; measure components hold what was observed.

Question 4 (O4): xmlschema.XMLSchema says DDICDIModels is not an element of the schema. Why?

B. The schema declares vc:minVersion="1.1". An XML Schema 1.0 processor honours that by ignoring the schema's content.

Question 5 (O5): What does a DDI-CDI link hold?

B. ddiReference gives the same three parts as a DDI-Lifecycle URN, and validType says which class to expect.

items.title: Cheat sheet
items.text: This page is a quick reference for the ddi-l package. Keep it open while you work through the modules or build your own projects.

items.title: The basics in 30 seconds
items.text:
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="My Survey", agency="example.org")
q = doc.add_question(text="How old are you?", label="Age question")
v = doc.add_variable(name="Age", question=q, label="Age in years")
doc.save("my-survey.xml")

That is enough to create a valid DDI document. Everything below adds detail.

label= is optional and worth the few characters: ddi lint reports every maintainable without one, so a document written without labels arrives warning about itself. Pass label_lang= when the label is in a different language from the name.

items.title: Create, open, and save
items.text: What you want to do Code Create a new study doc = ddi.new_study(title="...", agency="...") Open an existing file doc = ddi.open_ddi("file.xml") Open with validation doc = ddi.open_ddi("file.xml", validate=True) Save to disk doc.save("file.xml") Validate before saving errors = doc.validate()

items.title: Add items to a study
items.text:
# Questions
q = doc.add_question(text="What is your income?")

# Variables (linked to a question)
v = doc.add_variable(name="Income", question=q)

# Concepts
c = doc.add_concept(name="Economic Status")

# Universes
u = doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18+")

# Variables with concept and universe
v = doc.add_variable(name="Income", question=q, concept=c)

# Code lists
cl = doc.add_code_list(name="Gender Codes")

items.title: Variable types (representations)
items.text:
Say what kind of values a variable holds. Each setter returns the variable, so you can chain it onto add_variable:

doc.add_variable(name="age").set_numeric("Integer", low=0, high=120)
doc.add_variable(name="sex").set_coded(cl)  # values from a code list
doc.add_variable(name="comment").set_text()  # free text
doc.add_variable(name="dob").set_datetime("Date")

items.title: Count and list items
items.text:
print(len(doc.questions))  # Number of questions
print(len(doc.variables))  # Number of variables
print(len(doc.concepts))  # Number of concepts
print(len(doc.universes))  # Number of universes
print(len(doc.code_lists))  # Number of code lists

for q in doc.questions:
    print(q.identifier)

items.title: Find, remove, and add any type
items.text:
# Find an item by identifier
item = doc.find("my-identifier")

# Remove an item by identifier
doc.remove("my-identifier")

# Add any DDI type (Category, Instrument, etc.)
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

cat = doc.add_item(Category, name="Male")

# List all items of a type
for cat in doc.items(Category):
    print(cat.identifier)

items.title: Custom properties
items.text:
# Set a property
q.set_property("sensitivity", "high")

# Read a property
print(q.get_property("sensitivity"))  # "high"

# List all properties
print(q.properties)  # {"sensitivity": "high"}

# Remove a property
q.remove_property("sensitivity")

items.title: Custom fields (extend the standard)
items.text:
DDI is open: add organization-specific fields through the standard's own extension points, and they stay inside valid DDI and round-trip on save.

from ddi_l.models.base import UserID

# Namespace your keys so they never collide with another org's
v.set_property("myorg:retention_policy", "destroy after 7 years")
v.set_property("myorg:source_system", "CRM-2024")

# Back a custom field with a controlled vocabulary (references the code list URN)
quality = doc.add_code_list(name="Quality Flag Codes")  # a code list = the vocabulary
v.set_property("myorg:quality_flag", "validated")  # a value from the vocabulary
v.set_property("myorg:quality_flag_codes", quality)  # references the code list

# An organization-specific external identifier (value + type)
v.user_ids.append(UserID(value="CAT-000734", type_of_user_id="InternalCatalogue"))

# Audit which items carry your custom fields
tagged = [x for x in doc.variables if any(k.startswith("myorg:") for k in x.properties)]

Custom fields serialize to r:UserAttributePair (and r:UserID), which is still valid DDI. See Module 14.

items.title: Versioning
items.text:
item = doc.add_variable(name="age")  # or any DDI item

# Read the current version
print(item.version)  # "1": newly created items start at "1"

# Give it its next version
item.increment_version()  # 1 → 2

# Only if your organization uses dotted versions (major.minor.patch)
item.version = "1.0.0"
item.increment_major_version()  # 1.0.0 → 2.0.0
item.increment_minor_version()  # 2.0.0 → 2.1.0
item.increment_subversion()  # 2.1.0 → 2.1.1

# Record why you changed something
from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

item.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added income question for 2024 wave")]
    )
)
item.version_responsibility = "Survey Design Team"

Edit an item that is already in the file, then version it (see Module 15, sections 6 and 7):

question.question_texts[0].text = "In a typical week, do you work from home?"
question.increment_version()
variable.set_coded(new_code_list)  # switch to another code list
variable.increment_version()

# After a version bump, point references at the new version
variable.question_references = [
    question.to_reference() if ref.identifier == question.identifier else ref
    for ref in variable.question_references
]

items.title: Questionnaire flow constructs
items.text:
Questionnaire flow (the order questions are asked, and "skip" or "branch" rules) is built from these control constructs:

Construct What it does QuestionConstruct Wraps one question so it can sit in a flow Sequence Runs steps in order (step 1, step 2, step 3) IfThenElse Branches based on a condition (skip logic) StatementItem Shows a message instead of asking a question Instrument The whole questionnaire; points to the top sequence

You add each one with doc.add_item(...), and link them with .to_reference():

from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
    IfThenElse,
    StatementItem,
    Instrument,
)

q = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?")

# Wrap a question, then group constructs into an ordered section
qc_age = doc.add_item(
    QuestionConstruct, name="Ask Age", question_reference=q.to_reference()
)
section_a = doc.add_item(
    Sequence, name="Section A", control_construct_references=[qc_age.to_reference()]
)
section_c = doc.add_item(Sequence, name="Section C")

# Branch: run section A if true, section C if false
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Age gate")
gate.set_condition("age >= 18")
gate.then_construct_reference = section_a.to_reference()
gate.else_construct_reference = section_c.to_reference()

# Show a message; tie the whole thing together with an Instrument
doc.add_item(StatementItem, name="Welcome").set_text("Welcome to the survey")
doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Survey Instrument")

Loop works the same way (doc.add_item(Loop, name="...")), with its repeated section set via loop.control_construct_reference and how long it repeats via loop.set_condition(...). See Module 10 for the full worked example.

items.title: Data files (physical instances)
items.text:
A PhysicalInstance describes one real data file: where it lives and how big it is. Add it like any other item; it lives at the study level.

from ddi_l.models.physical import PhysicalInstance

pi = doc.add_item(PhysicalInstance, name="2021 Microdata File")
pi.set_data_file("https://example.org/health-2021.csv")  # where the file is
pi.set_record_count(15000)  # how many records

name becomes the file's citation title (a physical instance has no Name element in DDI).

To say where each variable sits in that file, add a record layout:

rl = doc.add_record_layout()
rl.add_data_item(age.to_reference(), start_position=1, width=2)
rl.add_data_item(income.to_reference(), start_position=3, width=8)

Omit the positions for a delimited (comma/tab) file.

To update many variables from a new data file, and version each change, see Module 15, "Going further".

items.title: Logical records and cubes
items.text:
# A logical record = which variables make up one case (one row)
dr = doc.add_data_relationship()
dr.add_logical_record()  # all variables, the usual rectangular file

# An NCube = multidimensional (cube) data: axes + measured values
cube = doc.add_ncube(name="Population by year and region")
cube.add_dimension(year.to_reference())
cube.add_dimension(region.to_reference())
cube.add_measure(population.to_reference())

# Attach an attribute to a specific region of the cube
region = cube.add_coordinate_region()
cube.add_dimension_value(region, rank=1, code_references=[code_2020.to_reference()])
cube.add_attribute(footnote.to_reference(), attachment_region=region)

Fine-grained physical and inline-data forms:

# Numeric range with inclusivity flags and missing values
age.set_numeric(
    "Integer",
    low=0,
    high=120,
    low_inclusive=True,
    high_inclusive=False,
    missing_values=["-9", "-8"],
)

# A data item's storage details in a fixed-width/delimited file
layout.add_data_item(
    age.to_reference(),
    start_position=1,
    width=3,
    storage_format="ASCII",
    delimiter="comma",
    decimal_positions=2,
)

# Inline data as a RecordSet (rows) or VariableSet (columns)
ds = doc.add_dataset(name="Sample rows")
ds.set_variable_order([age.to_reference(), sex.to_reference()])
ds.add_record(["42", "M"])
ds.add_variable_item(age.to_reference(), ["42", "37"])  # column form

# Harmonization: scheme-to-scheme and representation maps
cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="2020 to 2021")
cmp.add_managed_item_map(
    [(age_2020.to_reference(), age_2021.to_reference())], type_of_mapped_item="Variable"
)
cmp.add_representation_map(
    codes_2020.to_reference(), codes_2021.to_reference(), recode.to_reference()
)

items.title: Organize a study into a group
items.text:
# Wrap the study in a Group (a study series / publication package)
doc.add_group()
# The document stays editable; this still reaches the grouped study
doc.add_variable(name="region")

# Add more studies to the series, and map items across them
wave2 = doc.add_study(title="Wave 2")
# Edit a specific study via its cursor (doc.study() targets the primary)
doc.study(wave2.identifier).add_variable(name="income")
cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="2020 to 2021")
cmp.add_variable_map(age_2020.to_reference(), age_2021.to_reference())

items.title: Instance-level packages and translation
items.text:
# Archive-specific lifecycle metadata for the study
doc.add_archive()

# Reusable metadata shared across studies (a ResourcePackage)
doc.add_resource_package()

# A local holding of a deposited study (references the primary study by default)
doc.add_local_holding_package()

# Record which languages the instance was translated between
doc.add_translation_information(
    languages=["en", "fr"], description="Translated from French."
)

items.title: Data lineage (variable derivation)
items.text:
# Collection variable, linked to a question
v_age = doc.add_variable(name="age", question=q_age)

# Derived variable, linked to its source variable(s)
v_age_group = doc.add_variable(name="age_group")
v_age_group.source_variable_references = [v_age.to_reference()]

# Multi-source derivation
v_bmi = doc.add_variable(name="bmi")
v_bmi.source_variable_references = [v_height.to_reference(), v_weight.to_reference()]

items.title: Data linkage (combining datasets)
items.text:
Link records from two sources that share a common variable (the linkage key). Each source is its own study in a group, a Comparison records how the keys correspond, and linked variables trace back to both sources.

import ddi_l as ddi

# Source 1: survey (the primary study)
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Survey", agency="ca.statcan")
survey_key = doc.add_variable(name="anon_id")
survey_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")  # tag the common key
survey_health = doc.add_variable(name="health_rating")

# Source 2: admin register (a second study in the group)
admin = doc.add_study(title="Admin register")
admin_ds = doc.study(admin.identifier)
admin_key = admin_ds.add_variable(name="anon_id")
admin_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")
admin_visits = admin_ds.add_variable(name="hospital_visits")

# Map the keys; record the linkage method and quality
cmp = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-Admin Linkage")
match = cmp.correspondence(commonality="Shared anonymized id.", weight=1.0)
cmp.add_variable_map(
    survey_key.to_reference(), admin_key.to_reference(), correspondence=match
)
cmp.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")  # or "probabilistic"
cmp.set_property("match_rate", "0.94")

# Linked variable: provenance to BOTH sources
linked = doc.add_variable(name="health_by_hospital_use")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    survey_health.to_reference(),
    admin_visits.to_reference(),
]

A reference to a variable of the other study is checked against the whole file, so saving does not warn. See Module 12.

items.title: Multi-language support
items.text:
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString

# Create a question in English (default)
q = doc.add_question(text="What is your age?", lang="en")

# Add a French translation
q.question_texts.append(InternationalString(text="Quel est votre âge ?", lang="fr"))

items.title: Read data from CSV or Excel
items.text:
Sample file: survey_sample.csv

import csv
import ddi_l as ddi

# From CSV
with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

# Question wording from the questionnaire; unlisted columns get no question
QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Survey", agency="example.org")
for col in columns:
    q = doc.add_question(text=QUESTIONS[col]) if col in QUESTIONS else None
    doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q)
doc.save("survey.xml")

# From Excel (requires pandas + openpyxl)
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_excel("survey.xlsx")
for col in df.columns:
    doc.add_variable(name=col)

items.title: CLI commands
items.text:
Run these in your terminal.

Command What it does ddi validate file.xml Check a file against the DDI schema ddi lint file.xml Run best-practice checks ddi to-json file.xml Convert DDI XML to JSON ddi from-json file.json -o file.xml Convert JSON back to DDI XML ddi roundtrip in.xml -o out.xml Read and re-write (tests fidelity) ddi versions file.xml Show version info from the file ddi spec validate spec.yaml Check a questionnaire spec (Module 16) ddi conform file.xml --spec spec.yaml Compare an instrument with its spec ddi conform file.xml --spec spec.yaml --semantics syntactic Compare gates by normal form only, as without the logic extra (Module 18) ddi serve Run the HTTP service on this machine, port 8000 (Module 19)

Exit code 0 means success. Exit code 1 means failure.

What you type What it gives you ddi.new_study() Create a new DDI study document ddi.open_ddi() Open a DDI XML file from disk ddi.Document The document object (returned by new_study and open_ddi) ddi.DDIDocument Advanced: full DDI instance with indexing ddi.DDIFragment Advanced: a DDI fragment (partial document) ddi.read_ddi() Advanced: parse DDI from file, bytes, or string ddi.write_ddi() Advanced: serialize DDI to file or bytes ddi.iter_variables() Advanced: stream variables from a large file ddi.iter_questions() Advanced: stream questions from a large file ddi.iterparse_ddi() Advanced: memory-efficient streaming parse ddi.__version__ The installed version number

These are building blocks used across all DDI types.

items.title: Build a complete study from a CSV
items.text:
import csv
import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Household Survey", agency="stats.example.org")
universe = doc.add_universe(name="All households in Canada")

QUESTIONS = {
    "age": "How old are you?",
    "gender": "What is your gender?",
    "income": "What was your total income last year, before taxes?",
    "education_level": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
}

with open("survey_sample.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for col in reader.fieldnames:
        q = doc.add_question(text=QUESTIONS[col]) if col in QUESTIONS else None
        concept = doc.add_concept(name=col.replace("_", " ").title())
        doc.add_variable(name=col, question=q, concept=concept)

errors = doc.validate()
if not errors:
    doc.save("household-survey.xml")
    print("Saved and valid.")

items.title: Open, enrich, version, and re-save
items.text:
import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

doc = ddi.open_ddi("survey-v1.xml")

q = doc.add_question(text="What is your email address?")
doc.add_variable(name="Email", question=q)

study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added email question for wave 2")]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Survey Team"

doc.validate()
doc.save("survey-v2.xml")

items.text:
• User guide: Full API walkthrough
  • Validation guide: Schema and lint details
  • CLI recipes: All command-line examples
  • Models reference: Advanced model layer
  • Training modules: Step-by-step curriculum
  • Other DDI standards: Module 20 converts DDI-Codebook with reuse in mind, Module 21 writes DDI-CDI

items.title: Instructor guide
items.text: This guide helps facilitators deliver the ddi-l training curriculum in classrooms, workshops, or online sessions. It also works for self-paced learners who want facilitation context.

items.title: Classroom vs. self-paced
items.text:
The curriculum works in both modes:

  • Classroom: An instructor demonstrates each concept live, then learners complete the exercises. Use the timing and facilitation tips below.
  • Self-paced: Learners read each module, follow the code examples, and check their work against the answer keys.

items.title: Suggested schedules
items.text:
The workshop rows add up the instructor-led times the modules give, and the self-paced row their self-paced times, without breaks or setup. The course overview gives both totals for each format.

Format Modules Time Covers Half-day workshop 1-5 3 h 20 min What metadata is, setup, a first study, variables, concepts and universes Full-day workshop 1-9 6 h 30 min All of Tier 1 (including opening files and validation), CSV to DDI and code lists Three-day intensive 1-17 16 h, about 5 h 20 min a day Full curriculum with capstone Self-paced One module per session 12 h 20 min to 12 h 50 min 17 sessions of 20 to 90 min, about 3 to 4 weeks

items.title: Using the learning objectives
items.text:
Every module opens with numbered learning objectives (O1, O2, ...), tags each exercise and quiz question with the objectives it practises, and ends with a Check yourself list, one line per objective. Use them to run each session:

  • Open with the objectives. Read the module's objectives aloud, or show the box, at the start of the session. Learners then know what they will be able to do by the end, and you know what to check.
  • Pick exercises by tag. Short on time? Choose one exercise per objective rather than the first few in the list. If a learner struggles with one objective, give them another exercise with the same tag.
  • Close with Check yourself as an exit ticket. In the last five minutes, learners tick the lines they can do. A line many learners leave unticked tells you what to revisit at the start of the next session. In Module 17, the rubric and the presentation do the same job.

items.title: Environment setup checklist
items.text:
Before the session, make sure every learner has:

  • Python 3.11 or newer installed
  • ddi-l installed (pip install ddi-l)
  • pandas and openpyxl installed (pip install pandas openpyxl)
  • A text editor or IDE (VS Code, PyCharm, or even Notepad)
  • The sample CSV file, survey_sample.csv (capstone tracks also use thesis-data.csv, health-survey.csv and census-data.csv)
  • A terminal or command prompt

Have a fallback plan: a cloud notebook (Google Colab, JupyterHub) or a pre-built container with everything installed.

items.title: Module 1: What is metadata?
items.text:
• Start with the "messy table" exercise before defining metadata. Let learners discover the problem.
  • For NSO audiences, use the census example. For students, use the thesis example.
  • FAIR principles: Walk through the Dr. Chen example in section 4. Ask learners which FAIR letter is hardest to achieve without a standard like DDI. Most will say Interoperable or Findable; use this to motivate the rest of the curriculum.
  • Time: 45 min including discussion.

items.title: Module 2: Set up your environment
items.text:
• Budget 30 min: environment issues are the #1 classroom time sink.
  • Walk around and help with PATH issues, wrong Python versions, and virtual environments.
  • If installs fail, switch to the fallback environment immediately.

items.title: Module 3: Create your first study
items.text:
• This is the "aha" moment. Type the code live and show the XML output.
  • Common mistake: forgetting quotes around strings.
  • Section 9 introduces doc.validate() and doc.lint(). Ask learners to run both at the end of every later module, before they save.
  • Time: 45 min with live demo.

items.title: Module 4: Variables and questions
items.text:
• Draw the mental model on a whiteboard: Question → Variable → Data column.
  • Common mistake: passing the question text string instead of the question object to question=.
  • Time: 40 min.

items.title: Module 5: Concepts and universes
items.text:
• Use a diagram: Universe = "who", Concept = "what", Variable = "how it is measured", Question = "how it is asked".
  • Time: 40 min.

items.title: Module 6: Open and modify files
items.text:
• This is the archivist workflow: receive → inspect → enrich → validate → save.
  • Time: 40 min.

items.title: Module 7: Validate from the command line
items.text:
• For NSO audiences, spend extra time on batch validation and exit codes.
  • Time: 40 min.

items.title: Module 8: From CSV/Excel to DDI
items.text:
• This is the most important module for researchers and NSO staff. Demonstrate the full workflow: open a CSV, run the script, show the DDI XML output.
  • Emphasize: the CSV is the data. The DDI XML is documentation about the data. They are two different files.
  • Skip the SQL section for non-technical audiences.
  • Time: 60 min with exercises.

items.title: Module 9: Code lists
items.text:
• Show a real-world code list (ISO country codes, employment classifications).
  • Common mistake: forgetting to import Category.
  • Time: 50 min.

items.title: Module 10: Questionnaire flows
items.text:
• Start with a paper spec on screen. Have learners circle questions, underline skip rules, and box repeat instructions before touching code.
  • Draw the flowchart on a whiteboard. Map each box to a DDI construct.
  • Key confusion: "Why both a Question and a QuestionConstruct?" Explain content vs. flow separation.
  • Time: 60 min.

items.title: Module 11: Data lineage
items.text:
• Use the "recipe" analogy: raw ingredients (collection), cooking (production), plated dish (master). Provenance is the recipe.
  • Draw the three-file pipeline. For each variable, ask learners to trace it back to the original question.
  • Clarify: question_references = "what was asked", source_variable_references = "what data was used to compute this".
  • The numeric-to-coded derivation (age → age_group) is the most relatable example for all audiences.
  • For NSO staff: this is audit trail documentation that regulators need.
  • Time: 75 min.

items.title: Module 12: Data linkage
items.text:
• Anchor with the burden argument: reuse the tax file instead of re-asking income. Linkage creates new information from existing data.
  • Draw two files sharing one column (anon_id): the linkage key.
  • Contrast deterministic (one reliable key) vs probabilistic (several noisy fields, weighted agreement, clerical review).
  • Stress that source_variable_references crossing study boundaries is the technical heart of linkage; the save-time warning is expected.
  • For NSO staff: connect to their own organization's linkage environment and approval rules (for example, linkages that are pre-approved and those that need a review).
  • Always end a linkage on de-identification and, often, synthetic data.
  • Time: 75 min.

items.title: Module 13: Properties, find, and validate
items.text:
• Demonstrate that custom properties survive XML round-trips.
  • Show passing a code list object as a property value (stores URN).
  • Common mistake: trying to find() by name instead of by identifier.
  • Time: 50 min.

items.title: Module 14: Custom fields
items.text:
• Open with the "side spreadsheet" problem: local metadata kept outside the file always drifts out of sync. Custom fields keep it in the DDI.
  • Make the openness point explicit: DDI provides a standardized extension point. Show the UserAttributePair XML so learners see it is still valid DDI.
  • Contrast with Module 13: that module taught the set_property mechanics; this one governs extensions: namespaces, catalogs, controlled values, audit.
  • Clarify UserID vs custom property: identify vs describe.
  • For NSO/archive staff: connect to real governance (retention schedules, security classifications, data stewards), and the Section 9 audit loop.
  • Caution: do not reinvent built-in DDI; custom fields are for genuine gaps.
  • Time: 55 min.

items.title: Module 15: Update and version
items.text:
• Key module for archivists and NSO staff managing long-running surveys.
  • Show the XML before and after versioning so learners see the version number and rationale in the file.
  • Time: 75 min.

items.title: Module 16: Advanced questionnaire specification
items.text:
• For spec writers and NSO staff who move from screen designs and workbooks to a spec that instruments are checked against.
  • Put the missing-answer table of section 2 on the board first, and let learners fill in the last row before you show it.
  • Stress that a gate kept in the tool's own code is a correct result, and that an undocumented format is never guessed: the operators to use are the ones the tool's documentation lists.
  • Time: 90 min.

items.title: Module 17: Capstone projects
items.text:
• Let learners choose their persona track. If in a mixed group, form teams by role.
  • Ask to see each learner's plan (objective O1) before they write code.
  • Budget 90 min including the 5-minute presentations at the end (O6). Tracks B and D record two techniques each and run longest.
  • Score with the self-assessment rubric in the module: 80 points for the skills every track shares, and 20 for the track's own techniques (flow, lineage, linkage, custom fields or specification).

items.title: Module 18 (optional): Decide gates exactly
items.text:
• For spec writers and testers who already took Module 16, on machines where the logic extra installs (it brings the Z3 solver).
  • Ask the room whether Module 16's two gates for Q6 are the same before you run decide(): the "don't know" answer is the lesson.

items.title: Module 1: What is metadata and why does it matter?
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Define metadata in one sentence and point to two pieces of metadata that describe a given table.
  • O2. List three questions a reader must answer before using an undocumented table.
  • O3. Describe what DDI is in two sentences and name two kinds of organizations that use it.
  • O4. Match each FAIR principle to one way DDI metadata supports it.
  • O5. State what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do.

Prerequisites: None.

Time: 30 min self-paced / 45 min instructor-led.

New in this module: no functions or commands yet. This module sets out the ideas the rest of the course builds on.

items.title: 1. What is metadata?
items.text:
Metadata is information about your data. Think of a library card catalog. The catalog does not contain the full text of every book. Instead, it tells you the title, author, subject, and where to find each book. Metadata does the same thing for data files. It tells you what the data is about without showing you all the data.

Here are a few examples of metadata:

  • The title of a survey.
  • The date the data was collected.
  • The meaning of each column in a table.

Without metadata, a data file is just rows and columns of numbers. No one knows what those numbers mean.

items.title: 2. Real-world example: a household survey table
items.text:
Look at the table below. It comes from a household survey.

Column A Column B Column C 34 Female 52 000 28 Male 41 000 45 Female 67 000 22 Male 29 000 51 Other 73 000

Without documentation you might ask:

  • What do the numbers in Column A mean? Ages? ID numbers?
  • Is Column C in dollars, euros, or another currency?
  • Who was surveyed? Adults only? Everyone?
  • When was the survey done?

With documentation we add metadata:

Age Gender Annual Income (CAD) 34 Female 52 000 28 Male 41 000 45 Female 67 000 22 Male 29 000 51 Other 73 000
  • Study title: Canadian Household Income Survey 2024
  • Population: Canadian adults aged 18 and older.
  • Collection period: January-March 2024.

Now the data makes sense. Metadata is the difference between confusion and clarity.

items.title: 3. What is DDI?
items.text:
DDI stands for Data Documentation Initiative. It is an international standard (a set of agreed-upon rules) for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets. Governments, universities, and research organizations around the world use DDI to document their data so that others can find it, understand it, and reuse it.

Key facts about DDI:

  • It is maintained by the DDI Alliance.
  • It uses XML (a structured text format) to store the documentation.
  • It covers the full life of a dataset, from planning and collection to archiving and sharing.

items.title: 4. How DDI makes data FAIR
items.text:
FAIR is a set of four principles that help people share and reuse data. The letters stand for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Re-usable. Good data should follow all four. DDI-Lifecycle helps you meet each one.

Principle What it means How DDI helps Findable People can search for and discover the data. DDI gives every item a unique identifier and stores structured fields like title, agency, and concepts. Data catalogs can index these fields so users find your dataset in a search. Accessible People can get the data and its documentation. DDI files are standard XML. Any tool that reads XML can open them. No special software is required. Interoperable Data works with other data and tools. DDI uses shared code lists and controlled vocabularies. When two surveys use the same code list for gender or employment status, their data can be combined and compared. Re-usable People understand the data well enough to use it correctly. DDI records who collected the data, when, how, and what each variable means. A researcher in another country can read the DDI file and know exactly what the data contains.

items.title: Example: FAIR in action
items.text:
Imagine Dr. Chen publishes a health survey to an open data repository. Without DDI metadata, a visitor sees a file called health-2024.csv and has no idea what is inside.

With DDI metadata:

  • Findable: The repository indexes the DDI title, concepts ("Physical Health", "Mental Health"), and agency ("health-research.example.org"). A student searching for "mental health survey data" finds it.
  • Accessible: The DDI XML file is published next to the CSV. Anyone can download both files with no login or special tool.
  • Interoperable: The DDI file uses a standard code list for gender (Male / Female / Other). Another team in France uses the same code list, so both datasets can be merged for cross-country analysis.
  • Re-usable: The DDI file says the data was collected from adults aged 18+ in 2024, that "bmi" is body mass index in kg/m², and that income is in Canadian dollars. A new researcher can use the data correctly without asking the original team.

Without DDI, the data sits in a file that nobody finds, nobody understands, and nobody reuses. With DDI, the data becomes a shared resource.

items.title: 5. What is ddi-l?
items.text:
ddi-l is a Python package (a tool you install and use in the Python programming language) that lets you create, read, update, and validate DDI documents. You do not need to know XML to use it. You write a few lines of Python, and ddi-l handles the XML for you.

What ddi-l can do:

  • Create a new DDI study with questions and variables.
  • Read an existing DDI file and inspect its contents.
  • Update a DDI document by adding or removing items.
  • Validate a document to make sure it follows the DDI rules.

What ddi-l does not do:

  • It does not collect answers. You still run your survey with your own survey tool; ddi-l describes the survey and its data.
  • It does not analyze your data. It does not compute averages or tables from the values in your data file. It records what those values mean.

items.title: 6. The big picture
items.text:
Here is the typical workflow when you use ddi-l:

flowchart LR
    A["Your data\n(CSV / Excel)"] --> B["Your script\n(Python + ddi-l)"]
    B --> C["DDI XML file"]
    C --> D["Validation"]
    D --> E["Archive / Publish"]
  1. You start with a data file (for example, a CSV or Excel spreadsheet).
  2. You write a short Python script that uses ddi-l to describe the data.
  3. ddi-l creates a DDI XML file.
  4. You validate the file to make sure everything is correct.
  5. You archive or publish the file so others can find and understand your data.

items.title: 7. Who uses DDI? Four stories
items.text:
Maya, university student. Maya just finished her thesis on student stress. She needs to deposit her survey data in the university's research repository. DDI metadata helps future students find and understand her dataset.

Dr. Chen, researcher. Dr. Chen runs a multi-country health study. He publishes data to an open repository. DDI makes his datasets discoverable and comparable across countries.

Fatima, archivist. Fatima manages a data collection at a national library. She uses DDI to catalog thousands of datasets so researchers can search and browse the collection.

Jean-Pierre, National Statistics Office (NSO) staff. Jean-Pierre works at a government statistics office. His team documents every census and survey with DDI so the public can access reliable, well-documented data.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
Scenario

You receive a data file with no documentation. The file has five rows and the columns are labeled A, B, and C. The values look like numbers and short words.

Exercise 1 (O2). Look at the table below.

A B C 34 Female 52000 28 Male 41000 45 Female 67000 22 Male 29000 51 Other 73000

Write down 3 questions a new person would need answered before they could use this data. For example: What does column A measure?

Expected output: a list of three questions.

Answer

Any three of these, or similar:

  1. What does each column mean? (Is A an age? In years or months?)
  2. What unit is column C in? (Dollars? Euros? Per year or per month?)
  3. Who was surveyed? (Students? Adults? Everyone?)
  4. When was the data collected?

Exercise 2 (O1). The same researcher now sends a documented version of another file:

Campus Sleep Study 2025. Collected in September 2025 from first-year students. sleep_hrs is the hours of sleep on a typical school night.

sleep_hrs 7 6 8
  1. Write a one-sentence definition of metadata.
  2. Name two pieces of metadata in this file, and one piece of data.

Expected output: one sentence, then three short items.

Answer
  1. Metadata is information that describes data: what it means, where it came from, and how it was collected.
  2. Metadata: any two of the title "Campus Sleep Study 2025", the collection date (September 2025), the population (first-year students), the column name sleep_hrs, or its meaning (hours of sleep on a typical school night). Data: any of the values 7, 6, or 8.

Exercise 3 (O4). Match each FAIR principle (1 to 4) with the DDI feature (a to d) that supports it.

FAIR principle DDI feature 1. Findable a. The DDI file records who was surveyed, when, and what each variable means. 2. Accessible b. Two surveys use the same DDI code list for employment status. 3. Interoperable c. A data catalog indexes the title, agency, and concepts stored in the DDI file. 4. Re-usable d. The DDI file is plain XML, published next to the data, that any XML tool can open.

Expected output: four pairs, such as 1-?.

Answer

1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a.

  • Findable (c): the catalog can only find what is described in structured fields.
  • Accessible (d): a standard, open format needs no special software.
  • Interoperable (b): a shared code list means the same code has the same meaning in both surveys, so the data can be combined.
  • Re-usable (a): a new user knows exactly what the data contains.

Exercise 4 (O3). A new colleague asks you: "What is DDI?" Write a two-sentence answer. Name two kinds of organizations that use it.

Expected output: two sentences.

Answer

For example: "DDI, the Data Documentation Initiative, is an international standard for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets in XML. National statistics offices, data archives, universities, and research teams use it so that others can find, understand, and reuse their data."

Any two of these kinds of organizations are correct: national statistics offices, data archives or national libraries, universities and their research repositories, research teams.

Exercise 5 (O5). For each task below, write does if ddi-l does it, or does not if it does not.

  1. Write a DDI XML file from a short Python script.
  2. Send a questionnaire to respondents and collect their answers.
  3. Check a DDI document against the DDI rules.
  4. Calculate the average income from the values in a CSV file.
  5. Open an existing DDI file and list its questions.

Then write one sentence that says what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do.

Expected output: five answers, then one sentence.

Answer

Does: 1, 3, and 5. Does not: 2 and 4.

For example: "ddi-l creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI metadata from Python, but it does not collect survey answers."

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): A spreadsheet has a column headed Age (years) with the values 34, 28, and 45. Which of these is metadata?

A. The value 34.

B. The header Age (years), which says what the values mean and their unit.

C. The sum of the three values.

D. The second row.

Answer

B. Metadata is information about data. The header tells you what the numbers mean and how they are measured. The values themselves, and anything computed from them, are data.

Question 2 (O2): A colleague sends a table with columns A, B, and C and no notes. Column C holds values like 52000. You want to report the average income. Which question must you answer first?

A. Which font was used to type the table?

B. How many rows does the file have?

C. What is the name of the file?

D. What does column C measure, and in which currency and period?

Answer

D. Without knowing that C is income, and whether it is in dollars or euros, per year or per month, any average you report could be wrong. The other questions do not change what the numbers mean.

Question 3 (O3): Which sentence best describes DDI?

A. An international standard for describing surveys, censuses, and datasets, used by national statistics offices, data archives, and universities.

B. A survey tool that sends questionnaires to respondents.

C. A Python package that computes statistics from data files.

D. A database that stores survey answers.

Answer

A. DDI is a standard: a set of agreed rules for documentation. Option C confuses DDI with tools; ddi-l is a Python package that works with DDI, and it does not compute statistics.

Question 4 (O4): Your survey and a survey in France use the same DDI code list for gender, so the two datasets can be merged. Which FAIR principle does this support most directly?

A. Findable

B. Accessible

C. Interoperable

D. Re-usable

Answer

C. Interoperable means data works with other data. A shared code list gives each code the same meaning in both datasets, so they can be combined and compared.

Question 5 (O4): A data catalog reads the title, agency, and concepts in your DDI file, so a search for 'mental health survey' lists your dataset. Which FAIR principle does this support?

A. Findable

B. Accessible

C. Interoperable

D. Re-usable

Answer

A. Findable means people can discover the data. Structured DDI fields give catalogs something reliable to index and search.

Question 6 (O5): Which of these tasks does ddi-l NOT do?

A. Create a DDI study from a Python script.

B. Collect answers from survey respondents.

C. Validate a DDI document against the DDI rules.

D. Open an existing DDI file and inspect its contents.

Answer

B. ddi-l works with metadata: it creates, reads, updates, and validates DDI documents. Collecting answers is the job of a survey tool.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can define metadata in one sentence and point to two pieces of metadata that describe a table. (O1)
  • I can list three questions a reader must answer before using an undocumented table. (O2)
  • I can describe DDI in two sentences and name two kinds of organizations that use it. (O3)
  • I can match each FAIR principle to one way DDI metadata supports it. (O4)
  • I can state what ddi-l does and one thing it does not do. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Opening activity: Start with the "messy table" exercise (Exercise 1). Give learners the unlabeled table and ask them to guess what the data means. This builds motivation for the rest of the module.
  • Audience adaptation: For the messy table, you can show a few rows of the course's sample datasets with the headers removed: census-data.csv for NSO audiences and thesis-data.csv for university students. Both come back in the Module 17 capstone.
  • Discussion prompt: Ask learners to share a time they received a file with no documentation. What questions did they have?
  • FAIR matching (Exercise 3): Ask which FAIR letter is hardest to achieve without a standard like DDI. Most will say Interoperable or Findable.
  • Closing: Reinforce that ddi-l makes documentation easy: you write Python, and the tool creates the standard XML for you.

items.title: Module 2: Set up your Python environment
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Run python --version and decide whether your Python is new enough for ddi-l (3.11 or newer).
  • O2. Install ddi-l, pandas, and openpyxl with pip and read the last line of the output to confirm the install.
  • O3. Run a two-line Python test that prints the installed ddi-l version.
  • O4. Run ddi --help and find the command that does a given task, such as validating a file.
  • O5. Choose a workspace (Python REPL, script file, or notebook) for a given task and give a one-sentence reason.

Prerequisites: Module 1

Time: 20 min self-paced / 30 min instructor-led.

New in this module: python --version, pip install, ddi --help, import ddi_l as ddi, ddi.__version__

items.title: 1. What you need: Python 3.11 or newer
items.text:
Python is a programming language. ddi-l runs inside Python, so you must have Python installed on your computer.

Open a terminal (also called a command prompt) and type:

python --version

You should see something like:

Python 3.12.3

The version number must be 3.11 or higher. Read the first two numbers: 3.12 is newer than 3.11, so it works; 3.10 or 3.9 is too old. If your version is older, visit https://www.python.org/downloads/ and install a newer version.

Common issue

On some systems the command is python3 instead of python. If python --version does not work, try python3 --version.

items.title: 2. Install ddi-l
items.text:
In your terminal, run:

pip install ddi-l

This command downloads ddi-l from the internet and installs it. The word pip is Python's package installer. It is the standard way to add new tools to your Python setup.

Next, install two helper packages you will need in later modules:

pip install pandas openpyxl
  • pandas is a popular tool for working with tables of data.
  • openpyxl lets Python read and write Excel files.

You can install everything in one line if you prefer:

pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl

The last line of the output tells you how it went:

  • Successfully installed followed by package names means pip installed them.
  • Requirement already satisfied means a package was already there, so pip had nothing to do.
  • A line starting with ERROR means the install failed. Read the message, fix the cause (often the Python version or a network problem), and run the command again.

items.title: 3a. Test the command-line tool
items.text:
ddi-l includes a command-line tool called ddi. Run:

ddi --help

You should see a list of available commands. This confirms the tool is installed and ready to use. Each command has a one-line description. The start of the list looks like this:

positional arguments:
    validate            Validate an XML document against the DDI schema.
    to-json             Convert a DDI instance document to JSON.
    ...

To find the command for a task, read the descriptions, not just the names. For example, the command that checks a file against the DDI rules is the one whose description says "Validate". You will use these commands in Module 7.

items.title: 3b. Test in Python
items.text:
Open a Python session by typing python in your terminal. Then type:

import ddi_l as ddi

print(ddi.__version__)

You should see a version number printed, such as 0.1.0 or later. This confirms that Python can find and load the ddi-l package.

If you see ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddi_l' instead, ddi-l is not installed in the Python you are running. Run pip install ddi-l again, using the same python or python3 command you used above (for example, python3 -m pip install ddi-l).

Type exit() to leave the Python session.

items.title: 4. Choose your workspace
items.text:
You can write Python code in several ways. Pick the one that feels most comfortable:

Workspace How to start Best for Python REPL Type python in the terminal. Quick tests and exploring. Script file Create a file like my_script.py. Saving your work. Jupyter Notebook Run jupyter notebook in terminal. Step-by-step exploration.
  • REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It is an interactive prompt where you type one line of Python at a time and see the result right away.
  • A script file is a plain text file ending in .py that you run all at once.
  • A Jupyter Notebook is a tool that lets you mix text, code, and output in one document. It is not installed with ddi-l: run pip install notebook first if you want to use one.

How to choose:

  • Use the REPL for a one-off check you do not need to keep, such as printing the version.
  • Use a script file when you want to keep your code and run it again from the top with one command, such as python my_script.py.
  • Use a notebook when you want to see notes, code, and output together, step by step, for example to walk a colleague through your work.

For this curriculum, any of the three options will work.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
Scenario

You are setting up a new laptop for a training workshop. You need to make sure Python and ddi-l are ready to go before the workshop starts.

Exercise 1 (O1). Run python --version (or python3 --version) in your terminal. Write down the version, and say whether it is new enough for ddi-l.

Expected output: one line such as Python 3.12.3, and a yes or no.

Answer

For example, Python 3.12.3: yes, because 3.12 is 3.11 or newer. If you see Python 3.10.12 or older, the answer is no: install a newer Python from https://www.python.org/downloads/ before you continue.

Exercise 2 (O2). Run the following command in your terminal:

pip install ddi-l pandas openpyxl

Paste the last line of the output, and say what it means.

Expected output: a line that starts with Successfully installed or Requirement already satisfied.

Answer

The last line starts with Successfully installed and lists ddi-l-... among the packages (the version may vary). If the packages were already installed, pip says Requirement already satisfied instead. Both mean you are ready. A line starting with ERROR means the install failed.

Exercise 3 (O3). Open a Python session and run:

import ddi_l as ddi

print(ddi.__version__)
