                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )


with open("thesis-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
columns = list(rows[0])

# Version 1
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Student Stress Survey 2024", agency="university.example.org")
# How each column was asked. StudentID is assigned and AnxietyScore is computed
# from a questionnaire, so neither gets a question of its own.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Age": "How old are you?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "YearOfStudy": "What year of your program are you in?",
    "Program": "Which program are you enrolled in?",
    "StudyHours": "On a typical day, how many hours do you study?",
    "SleepHours": "On a typical night, how many hours do you sleep?",
    "WorkHours": "How many hours a week do you work for pay?",
    "ExerciseDays": "On how many days last week did you exercise?",
    "StressLevel": "On a scale of 1 to 10, how stressed have you felt this term?",
    "SoughtSupport": "Have you sought support from campus services this term?",
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}

# One code list per coded column, from the values in the file
for col in ("Gender", "Program", "SoughtSupport"):
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col} Codes")
    add_codes(doc, code_list, sorted({row[col] for row in rows}))
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
doc.add_concept(name="Academic Workload")
doc.add_concept(name="Well-Being")
doc.add_universe(name="Undergraduate students aged 18-25")
variables["StudyHours"].set_property("dataSource", "Online survey tool")
variables["AnxietyScore"].set_property(
    "scoring", "Sum of a standard 10-item anxiety scale"
)

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v1: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
doc.save("thesis-v1.xml")

# Version 2: a derived variable and its lineage
doc = ddi.open_ddi("thesis-v1.xml")
by_name = {v.names[0].text: v for v in doc.variables}
stress_index = doc.add_variable(name="StressIndex")
stress_index.source_variable_references = [
    by_name["StressLevel"].to_reference(),
    by_name["AnxietyScore"].to_reference(),
]

study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(text="Added the derived StressIndex variable")
        ]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Thesis Author"

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v2: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
# -> v2: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("thesis-v2.xml")

items.title: Track B: Researcher: Package a Health Survey for Publication
items.text:
Scenario

You lead a multi-country health study. Your data file has 15 columns of survey data. Your team also linked each respondent to a hospital admissions register. You need to package the metadata for an open data repository.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. (O1) Plan the project and read the data. Start from a data file with at least 15 columns. Download the sample health survey (40 respondents, 15 columns) or use your own. Fill in the plan table, then read the column names:

    Download health-survey.csv

    import csv

import ddi_l as ddi

with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="International Health Survey 2024",
    agency="health-research.example.org",
)
print(f"{len(columns)} columns")  # -> 15 columns

    If your data is in an Excel workbook, read the column names with pandas instead (see Module 8):

    import pandas as pd

columns = list(pd.read_excel("health-survey.xlsx").columns)

  2. (O2) Create the questions and variables from the columns. The first line below creates one question per entry of QUESTIONS. The second creates one variable per column and links it to its question. questions.get(col) gives None for a column with no question, such as RespondentID.

    # Copy the wording from your questionnaire. Columns left out, such as
# RespondentID, become variables without a question.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Age": "How old are you?",
    "SmokingStatus": "Which of these best describes your smoking?",
    "ExerciseFrequency": "How often do you exercise for at least 30 minutes?",
    "SelfRatedHealth": "In general, how would you rate your health?",
    # ...one entry for each column you asked about
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 15

  3. (O2) Add 4 concepts and a universe:

    doc.add_concept(name="Physical Health")
doc.add_concept(name="Mental Health")
doc.add_concept(name="Access to Healthcare")
doc.add_concept(name="Demographics")
doc.add_universe(name="Adults aged 18 and over in the participating countries")

  4. (O2) Add 2 code lists built from the values in the file. A code list is a set of allowed answers (like "Yes", "No", "Unsure"). {row[col] for row in rows} collects the distinct values of a column; each one becomes a category and a code, and set_coded() points the variable at the list.

    from uuid import uuid4

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

for col in ["SmokingStatus", "ExerciseFrequency"]:
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col} Codes")
    for number, label in enumerate(sorted({row[col] for row in rows}), start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> Code lists: 2

  5. (O4) Record lineage. Body mass index (BMI) is computed from height and weight. It gets no question; it lists its two sources instead (see Module 11):

    bmi = doc.add_variable(name="BMI", label="Body mass index")
bmi.source_variable_references = [
    variables["HeightCm"].to_reference(),
    variables["WeightKg"].to_reference(),
]

  6. (O4) Record the linkage. Your team joined the survey to a hospital admissions register on RespondentID. Record it as in Module 12: the register is a second study, the key is tagged on both sides, a Comparison maps the keys, and the linked variable names its sources in both studies.

    register = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2024")
register_ds = doc.study(register.identifier)
register_key = register_ds.add_variable(name="RespondentID")
admissions = register_ds.add_variable(name="HospitalAdmissions")

variables["RespondentID"].set_property("linkage_role", "key")
register_key.set_property("linkage_role", "key")

link = doc.add_comparison(name="Survey-to-register linkage 2024")
exact = link.correspondence(
    commonality="The same respondent identifier in both sources.",
    weight=1.0,
)
link.add_variable_map(
    variables["RespondentID"].to_reference(),
    register_key.to_reference(),
    correspondence=exact,
)
link.set_property("linkage_method", "deterministic")

linked = doc.add_variable(name="HealthByHospitalUse")
linked.source_variable_references = [
    variables["SelfRatedHealth"].to_reference(),
    admissions.to_reference(),
]
print(f"Comparisons: {len(doc.comparisons)}")  # -> Comparisons: 1

  7. (O3) Validate and lint the document:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"Validation errors: {len(errors)}, lint errors: {len(lint_errors)}")
# -> Validation errors: 0, lint errors: 0

  8. (O3) Save as version 1:

    doc.save("health-survey-v1.xml")

    Then export it to JSON from the command line:

    ddi to-json health-survey-v1.xml --indent 2 --output health-survey-v1.json

  9. (O5) Update to version 2 with a rationale. Add a new variable or fix a label.

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

q_dentist = doc.add_question(
    text="How many times did you see a dentist in the last 12 months?"
)
doc.add_variable(name="DentistVisitsLastYear", question=q_dentist)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added dental visit frequency question")]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Principal Investigator"
doc.save("health-survey-v2.xml")

    Check the new file from the command line with ddi validate health-survey-v2.xml.

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
• Your plan: one row per column, and the three notes.
  • health-survey-v1.xml: valid DDI document, with BMI's lineage and the linkage to the register.
  • health-survey-v1.json: JSON export of the document.
  • health-survey-v2.xml: updated version with rationale.
Sample solution

One complete script, using health-survey.csv. Run ddi to-json health-survey-v1.xml --indent 2 --output health-survey-v1.json after it.

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem


def add_codes(doc, code_list, labels):

with open("health-survey.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:

QUESTIONS = {

    "Age": "How old are you?",
    "Sex": "What is your sex?",

questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {

for col in ("SmokingStatus", "ExerciseFrequency"):

for name in (

# Lineage: BMI is computed from height and weight
bmi = doc.add_variable(name="BMI", label="Body mass index")
bmi.source_variable_references = [

# Linkage: the register is a second study, joined on RespondentID
register = doc.add_study(title="Hospital Admissions Register 2024")

register_key = register_ds.add_variable(name="RespondentID")
admissions = register_ds.add_variable(name="HospitalAdmissions")
variables["RespondentID"].set_property("linkage_role", "key")

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v1: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
# -> v1: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("health-survey-v1.xml")

# Version 2
dentist = doc.add_question(
    text="How many times did you see a dentist in the last 12 months?"
)

study.increment_version()

items.title: Track C: Archivist: Enrich and Version Existing DDI Files
items.text:
Scenario

You manage a data collection at a national library. You receive 3 DDI files from different research teams. Some files are missing metadata. You need to check each file, add what is missing, record the archive's own facts about it, and create new versions.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. (O1) Prepare 3 DDI files and plan. Use files from earlier modules, or create 3 small studies now. Your plan has one row per file: what it holds, what is missing, and what you will add.

    import ddi_l as ddi

questions = [
    "How old are you?",
    "How many people live in your household?",
    "Did you vote in the last federal election?",
]
for i, text in enumerate(questions, start=1):
    doc = ddi.new_study(
        title=f"Research Study {i}",
        agency="library.example.org",
    )
    doc.add_question(text=text)
    doc.add_variable(name=f"Var{i}")
    doc.save(f"study-{i}.xml")

  2. (O3) For each file, check completeness. Open the file and list what it contains. The last line counts the variables linked to a question:

    doc = ddi.open_ddi("study-1.xml")
print(f"Questions:  {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables:  {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"Concepts:   {len(doc.concepts)}")
print(f"Universes:  {len(doc.universes)}")
print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")
linked = sum(1 for v in doc.variables if v.question_references)
print(f"Variables linked to a question: {linked}")
# -> Variables linked to a question: 0

  3. (O2) Add missing metadata. If a file has no concepts, add one. If it has no universe, add one. If a variable is not linked to its question, link it. If a question has a fixed set of answers, such as the vote question in study 3, add a code list with categories and point the variable at it (the sample solution shows how).

    doc.add_concept(name="Social Sciences")
doc.add_universe(name="General population")

# Link the variable to the question it records
variable, question = doc.variables[0], doc.questions[0]
variable.question_references = [question.to_reference()]

  4. (O4) Add custom fields from a catalog. Your archive records the same facts about every file it accepts. Write them down once as a catalog: one namespace (archive:) and the meaning of each key (see Module 14). Set fields only through a function that checks the catalog, so a typo cannot create a new key. Then audit the file: count the items that carry your fields.

    ARCHIVE_FIELDS = {
    "archive:accession_date": "Date the archive received the file.",
    "archive:depositor": "Team that deposited the file.",
    "archive:retention": "How long the archive keeps the file.",
    "archive:access": "Who may use the data: open, registered or restricted.",
}


def set_archive_field(item, key, value):
    if key not in ARCHIVE_FIELDS:
        raise KeyError(f"{key!r} is not in the archive catalog")
    item.set_property(key, value)


def count_archive_fields(doc):
    items = [doc.study_unit, *doc.questions, *doc.variables]
    return sum(
        any(key.startswith("archive:") for key in item.properties) for item in items
    )


study = doc.study_unit
set_archive_field(study, "archive:accession_date", "2024-11-04")
set_archive_field(study, "archive:depositor", "Research team 1")
set_archive_field(study, "archive:retention", "permanent")
set_archive_field(variable, "archive:access", "open")
print(f"Items with archive fields: {count_archive_fields(doc)}")
# -> Items with archive fields: 2

  5. (O5) Give the study its next version, with a rationale:

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(
                text="Enriched metadata: added concept, universe, question link and archive fields"
            )
        ]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Archive Metadata Team"

  6. (O3) Validate, lint and save:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
if not errors and not lint_errors:
    doc.save("study-1-enriched.xml")
    print("Saved study-1-enriched.xml")  # -> Saved study-1-enriched.xml

  7. Repeat steps 2 to 6 for all 3 files.

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
• Your plan: one row per file.
  • 3 updated XML files (study-1-enriched.xml, study-2-enriched.xml, study-3-enriched.xml), all valid, each with a version rationale.
  • Your custom-field catalog, and the audit count for each file.
Sample solution

One loop over the three files from step 1.

from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

ARCHIVE_FIELDS = {
    "archive:accession_date": "Date the archive received the file.",
    "archive:depositor": "Team that deposited the file.",
    "archive:retention": "How long the archive keeps the file.",
    "archive:access": "Who may use the data: open, registered or restricted.",
}
YES_NO_FILES = {3}  # from the plan: study 3 asks a yes/no question


def set_archive_field(item, key, value):
    if key not in ARCHIVE_FIELDS:
        raise KeyError(f"{key!r} is not in the archive catalog")
    item.set_property(key, value)


def count_archive_fields(doc):
    items = [doc.study_unit, *doc.questions, *doc.variables]
    return sum(
        any(key.startswith("archive:") for key in item.properties) for item in items
    )


for i in (1, 2, 3):
    doc = ddi.open_ddi(f"study-{i}.xml")
    if not doc.concepts:
        doc.add_concept(name="Social Sciences")
    if not doc.universes:
        doc.add_universe(name="General population")
    variable, question = doc.variables[0], doc.questions[0]
    if not variable.question_references:
        variable.question_references = [question.to_reference()]
    if i in YES_NO_FILES:
        yes_no = doc.add_code_list(name="Yes/No")
        for value, label in (("1", "Yes"), ("2", "No")):
            category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
            yes_no.codes.append(
                CodeItem(
                    agency=yes_no.agency,
                    identifier=str(uuid4()),
                    version=yes_no.version,
                    value=value,
                    category=category.to_reference(),
                )
            )
        variable.set_coded(yes_no)

    study = doc.study_unit
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:accession_date", "2024-11-04")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:depositor", f"Research team {i}")
    set_archive_field(study, "archive:retention", "permanent")
    set_archive_field(variable, "archive:access", "open")

    study.increment_version()
    study.version_rationales.append(
        VersionRationale(
            descriptions=[
                InternationalString(
                    text="Enriched metadata: added concept, universe, question link and archive fields"
                )
            ]
        )
    )
    study.version_responsibility = "Archive Metadata Team"

    lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
    print(
        f"study-{i}: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, "
        f"{len(lint_errors)} lint errors, "
        f"{count_archive_fields(doc)} items with archive fields"
    )
    doc.save(f"study-{i}-enriched.xml")
# -> study-3: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors, 2 items with archive fields

items.title: Track D: NSO Staff: Build a Census Instrument
items.text:
Scenario

You work at a national statistics office. Your census team has a large CSV file with 20+ columns. You need to build a complete DDI document, create code lists from the data, describe the questionnaire's flow and write its specification, manage multiple versions, and automate validation with a script (bash, or PowerShell on Windows).

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. (O1) Plan the project and read the data. Start from a large CSV with 20+ columns. Download the sample census extract (55 people in 20 households, 22 columns, including the five coded columns used in step 3) or use your own. Fill in the plan table. Note that EmploymentType says "Not applicable" for children: that is a gate, which step 5 records.

    Download census-data.csv

    import csv

import ddi_l as ddi

with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    columns = csv.DictReader(f).fieldnames

doc = ddi.new_study(
    title="National Census 2024",
    agency="ca.statcan",
)
print(f"{len(columns)} columns")  # -> 22 columns

  2. (O2) Create 20+ variables from the CSV columns, each linked to its question:

    # Wording from the census questionnaire. HouseholdID and PersonNumber are
# assigned, not asked, so they are left out and get no question.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Province": "In which province or territory do you live?",
    "Age": "What was your age at your last birthday?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "MaritalStatus": "What is your marital status?",
    "EmploymentType": "Last week, were you an employee, self-employed, or not working?",
    "HousingType": "What type of dwelling do you live in?",
    # ...one entry for each remaining column
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")  # -> Variables: 22

  3. (O2) Build 5 code lists from the values in the file, each with one category and one code per value:

    from uuid import uuid4

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem

with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

categorical_cols = [
    "Province",
    "Gender",
    "MaritalStatus",
    "EmploymentType",
    "HousingType",
]
for col in categorical_cols:
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col}Codes")
    for number, label in enumerate(sorted({row[col] for row in rows}), start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

print(f"Code lists: {len(doc.code_lists)}")  # -> Code lists: 5

  4. (O2) Add concepts, a universe and custom properties. Set custom properties, such as a classification, on at least 2 items:

    doc.add_concept(name="Population")
doc.add_concept(name="Labour")
doc.add_universe(name="All persons usually resident in private dwellings")

variables["Occupation"].set_property("classification", "ISCO-08")
variables["AnnualIncome"].set_property("referencePeriod", "Calendar year 2023")

  5. (O4) Build the questionnaire flow. Everyone answers the person questions. Only people aged 15 and over answer the labour questions. Build the flow as in Module 10: a QuestionConstruct for each question, a Sequence for each section, an IfThenElse for the gate, and an Instrument that points at the main sequence.

    from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    IfThenElse,
    Instrument,
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
)

AGE_GATE = "Age >= 15"


def ask(col):
    """A QuestionConstruct that asks the question of column col."""
    return doc.add_item(
        QuestionConstruct, name=col, question_reference=questions[col].to_reference()
    )


person = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="person",
    control_construct_references=[
        ask("Age").to_reference(),
        ask("Gender").to_reference(),
    ],
)
labour = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="labour",
    control_construct_references=[ask("EmploymentType").to_reference()],
)
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Working-age gate")
gate.set_condition(AGE_GATE, description="Persons aged 15 and over")
gate.then_construct_reference = labour.to_reference()

main = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Census flow",
    control_construct_references=[person.to_reference(), gate.to_reference()],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Census 2024 questionnaire")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main.to_reference()
print(f"Instruments: {len(doc.items(Instrument))}")  # -> Instruments: 1

  6. (O4) Write the specification. A spec says what the instrument must contain: its modules, their questions and the gates (see Module 16). Write it to a file, load it, and check that its gate says the same as the instrument's.

    from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, load_spec

SPEC = """\
spec: census-2024
version: "1"
code_lists:
  Employment:
    values: {1: Employee, 2: Self-employed, 3: Unemployed, 4: Not in labour force}
modules:
  - id: person
    questions:
      - id: Age
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 120, decimals: 0}}
  - id: labour
    gate: Age >= 15
    questions:
      - id: EmploymentType
        domain: {code: {list: Employment}}
"""
Path("census.spec.yaml").write_text(SPEC, encoding="utf-8")

spec = load_spec("census.spec.yaml")
labour_gate = spec.module("labour").gate_text
print(labour_gate, equivalent(labour_gate, AGE_GATE))  # -> Age >= 15 True
print(equivalent(AGE_GATE, "not Age < 15"))  # -> False

    Decide what the gate does when Age has no answer, and write it in your plan. Age >= 15 is false when Age is missing, so a person with no age skips the labour questions. not Age < 15 would ask them, which is why equivalent() says the two differ. "Not applicable" is not in the spec's code list: it is what the data holds for people the gate skipped.

    Check the spec file from the command line too:

    ddi spec validate census.spec.yaml

  7. (O3) Validate, lint and save as version 1:

    errors = doc.validate()
lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"Validation errors: {len(errors)}, lint errors: {len(lint_errors)}")
# -> Validation errors: 0, lint errors: 0
doc.save("census-v1.xml")

  8. (O5) Update to version 2: add a new question and variable:

    from ddi_l.models.base import VersionRationale, InternationalString

q_internet = doc.add_question(text="Do you have access to high-speed internet?")
doc.add_variable(name="HighSpeedInternet", question=q_internet)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[InternationalString(text="Added internet access question")]
    )
)
study.version_responsibility = "Census Content Team"
doc.save("census-v2.xml")

  9. (O5) Update to version 3: a redesign (add 5 new questions, retire 3 old ones). Retiring a question also retires the variable that recorded its answers; otherwise the variable would keep pointing at a question that is no longer in the file (see Module 15). Retire only questions the flow does not use. A version holds one rationale, so replace the one from version 2; census-v2.xml keeps it.

    # Add new questions
for text in [
    "What is your primary language at home?",
    "Do you identify as Indigenous?",
    "What is your highest degree?",
    "Do you have a disability?",
    "What is your annual household income?",
]:
    doc.add_question(text=text)

# Retire 3 old questions, and the variables that recorded their answers
for col in ["Province", "MaritalStatus", "HousingType"]:
    doc.remove(variables[col].identifier)
    doc.remove(questions[col].identifier)

study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales = [
    VersionRationale(
        descriptions=[
            InternationalString(
                text="Major redesign: added equity and income questions"
            )
        ]
    )
]
errors = [finding for finding in doc.lint() if finding.severity == "error"]
print(f"Lint errors: {len(errors)}")  # -> Lint errors: 0
print(f"Validation errors: {len(doc.validate())}")  # -> Validation errors: 0
doc.save("census-v3.xml")

  10. (O3) Batch validate all three files from the command line:

    ddi validate census-v1.xml
ddi validate census-v2.xml
ddi validate census-v3.xml

  11. (O3) Write a script that runs the full pipeline, in bash:

    #!/bin/bash
# validate.sh: check the spec, then validate all census DDI files.

echo "=== Checking the spec ==="
ddi spec validate census.spec.yaml

echo "=== Validating census files ==="
for f in census-v*.xml; do
    echo "--- $f ---"
    ddi validate "$f"
    if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
        echo "PASS"
    else
        echo "FAIL"
    fi
    echo ""
done
echo "=== Done ==="

    Make the script executable and run it:

    chmod +x validate.sh
./validate.sh

    On Windows, write the same script in PowerShell as validate.ps1:

    # validate.ps1: check the spec, then validate all census DDI files.

Write-Output "=== Checking the spec ==="
ddi spec validate census.spec.yaml

Write-Output "=== Validating census files ==="
foreach ($f in Get-ChildItem census-v*.xml) {
    Write-Output "--- $($f.Name) ---"
    ddi validate $f.Name
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { Write-Output "PASS" } else { Write-Output "FAIL" }
    Write-Output ""
}
Write-Output "=== Done ==="

    and run it with powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File validate.ps1 (Windows does not run script files by default).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
• Your plan: one row per column, the three notes, and what the gate does with a missing age.
  • census-v1.xml: version 1, valid, with the instrument and its gate.
  • census.spec.yaml: the specification, passing ddi spec validate.
  • census-v2.xml: version 2, valid, with rationale.
  • census-v3.xml: version 3, valid, with rationale.
  • validate.sh (or validate.ps1 on Windows): script that checks the spec and validates all files.
Sample solution

One complete script, using census-data.csv. Run validate.sh (or validate.ps1) from step 11 after it.

import csv
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import ddi_l as ddi
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale
from ddi_l.models.datacollection import (
    IfThenElse,
    Instrument,
    QuestionConstruct,
    Sequence,
)
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category, CodeItem
from ddi_l.spec import equivalent, load_spec


def add_codes(doc, code_list, labels):
    """Add one Category and one Code per label, numbered from 1."""
    for number, label in enumerate(labels, start=1):
        category = doc.add_item(Category, name=label, label=label)
        code_list.codes.append(
            CodeItem(
                agency=code_list.agency,
                identifier=str(uuid4()),
                version=code_list.version,
                value=str(number),
                category=category.to_reference(),
            )
        )


def rationale(text):
    return VersionRationale(descriptions=[InternationalString(text=text)])


with open("census-data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
columns = list(rows[0])

doc = ddi.new_study(title="National Census 2024", agency="ca.statcan")
# HouseholdID and PersonNumber are assigned, not asked.
QUESTIONS = {
    "Province": "In which province or territory do you live?",
    "Age": "What was your age at your last birthday?",
    "Gender": "What is your gender?",
    "MaritalStatus": "What is your marital status?",
    "RelationshipToHead": "What is your relationship to Person 1?",
    "CountryOfBirth": "In which country were you born?",
    "Citizenship": "Of what country are you a citizen?",
    "MotherTongue": "What language did you first learn at home in childhood?",
    "HighestEducation": "What is the highest level of education you have completed?",
    "EmploymentType": "Last week, were you an employee, self-employed, or not working?",
    "Occupation": "What was your main kind of work last week?",
    "WeeklyHoursWorked": "How many hours did you work last week?",
    "AnnualIncome": "What was your total income last year?",
    "CommuteMode": "How did you usually get to work last week?",
    "HousingType": "What type of dwelling do you live in?",
    "Tenure": "Is this dwelling owned or rented by a member of this household?",
    "Rooms": "How many rooms are in this dwelling?",
    "YearBuilt": "In what year was this dwelling built?",
    "HouseholdSize": "How many people usually live here?",
    "InternetAccess": "Does this household have access to the internet at home?",
}
questions = {col: doc.add_question(text=text) for col, text in QUESTIONS.items()}
variables = {
    col: doc.add_variable(name=col, question=questions.get(col)) for col in columns
}

for col in ("Province", "Gender", "MaritalStatus", "EmploymentType", "HousingType"):
    code_list = doc.add_code_list(name=f"{col}Codes")
    add_codes(doc, code_list, sorted({row[col] for row in rows}))
    variables[col].set_coded(code_list)

doc.add_concept(name="Population")
doc.add_concept(name="Labour")
doc.add_universe(name="All persons usually resident in private dwellings")
variables["Occupation"].set_property("classification", "ISCO-08")
variables["AnnualIncome"].set_property("referencePeriod", "Calendar year 2023")

# The flow: everyone answers the person section; the labour section has a gate
AGE_GATE = "Age >= 15"


def ask(col):
    return doc.add_item(
        QuestionConstruct, name=col, question_reference=questions[col].to_reference()
    )


person = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="person",
    control_construct_references=[ask(c).to_reference() for c in ("Age", "Gender")],
)
labour = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="labour",
    control_construct_references=[
        ask(c).to_reference()
        for c in ("EmploymentType", "Occupation", "WeeklyHoursWorked")
    ],
)
gate = doc.add_item(IfThenElse, name="Working-age gate")
gate.set_condition(AGE_GATE, description="Persons aged 15 and over")
gate.then_construct_reference = labour.to_reference()
main = doc.add_item(
    Sequence,
    name="Census flow",
    control_construct_references=[person.to_reference(), gate.to_reference()],
)
instrument = doc.add_item(Instrument, name="Census 2024 questionnaire")
instrument.control_construct_reference = main.to_reference()

# The spec of the same flow. A person with no age skips the labour section.
Path("census.spec.yaml").write_text(
    """\
spec: census-2024
version: "1"
modules:
  - id: person
    questions:
      - id: Age
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 120, decimals: 0}}
  - id: labour
    gate: Age >= 15
    questions:
      - id: EmploymentType
        domain: {text: {max_length: 40}}
      - id: Occupation
        domain: {text: {max_length: 60}}
      - id: WeeklyHoursWorked
        domain: {numeric: {min: 0, max: 168, decimals: 0}}
""",
    encoding="utf-8",
)
spec = load_spec("census.spec.yaml")
print(f"Gates agree: {equivalent(spec.module('labour').gate_text, AGE_GATE)}")
# -> Gates agree: True

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v1: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
doc.save("census-v1.xml")

# Version 2: one question added
q_internet = doc.add_question(text="Do you have access to high-speed internet?")
doc.add_variable(name="HighSpeedInternet", question=q_internet)
study = doc.study_unit
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales.append(rationale("Added internet access question"))
study.version_responsibility = "Census Content Team"
doc.save("census-v2.xml")

# Version 3: five questions added, three retired with their variables
for text in [
    "What is your primary language at home?",
    "Do you identify as Indigenous?",
    "What is your highest degree?",
    "Do you have a disability?",
    "What is your annual household income?",
]:
    doc.add_question(text=text)
for col in ("Province", "MaritalStatus", "HousingType"):
    doc.remove(variables[col].identifier)
    doc.remove(questions[col].identifier)
study.increment_version()
study.version_rationales = [
    rationale("Major redesign: added equity and income questions")
]

lint_errors = [f for f in doc.lint() if f.severity == "error"]
print(f"v2: {len(doc.validate())} validation errors, {len(lint_errors)} lint errors")
# -> v2: 0 validation errors, 0 lint errors
doc.save("census-v3.xml")

items.title: Present your project
items.text:
(O6) Finish with a 5-minute presentation to your group. If you work alone, write the same content as a one-page note. Keep to this order:

  1. The data and its readers (30 seconds): what the data is, and who will read the metadata.
  2. The plan (1 minute): show your plan table, and say which techniques your track needed.
  3. The proof (1 minute): run ddi validate on your last file. Show one place in the XML where your technique is recorded, such as a SourceVariableReference, a Comparison, a UserAttributePair or an IfThenElse.
  4. Two design choices (2 minutes): for each one, say what you chose, the option you rejected, and why.
  5. One thing you would change next time (30 seconds).

Choices worth justifying:

  • Coded or free text for a column such as Program or Occupation.
  • Which columns get a question, and which are assigned or computed.
  • What your version rationale says, and whether answers stay comparable.
  • A custom field, or a field DDI already has.
  • What a gate does when the answer it tests is missing (Track D).

items.title: Capstone checklist (for all tracks)
items.text:
Use this checklist to make sure your project is complete:

  • A written plan covers every column (Track C: every file) and names your track's techniques.
  • The document starts from a CSV or Excel file (Track C: from the DDI files you received).
  • Every variable a respondent answered is linked to its question.
  • Coded columns use code lists with categories.
  • At least one concept and one universe are defined.
  • Custom properties are set on at least 2 items.
  • Questionnaire flow (Track D): an Instrument points at a main Sequence that holds an IfThenElse gate.
  • Lineage (Tracks A and B): every derived variable lists its sources in source_variable_references.
  • Linkage (Track B): the register is a second study, the key is tagged on both sides, and a Comparison maps the keys.
  • Custom fields (Track C): every key comes from your catalog, and the audit counts the items that carry one.
  • Specification (Track D): the spec passes ddi spec validate, and its gate matches the instrument's.
  • The version was incremented at least once, with a rationale and a responsibility.
  • Document passes doc.validate() and doc.lint() with no errors.
  • Every saved file passes ddi validate.
  • Two design choices are ready to present.

items.title: Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Use this table to score your own work, or a partner's. The rubric measures the six objectives of this module on your track's data. The maximum score is 100 points.

Criteria Objective Modules Points A plan, written before the code, covers every column and names your track's techniques O1 8 10 Every asked column is a variable linked to its question; assigned and computed columns have none O2 4, 8 10 At least one concept and one universe O2 5 5 Coded columns use code lists with categories O2 9 10 Custom properties on at least 2 items O2 13 5 No errors from doc.validate(), doc.lint() or ddi validate on any saved file O3 3, 7, 13 15 Your track's techniques (next table) O4 10, 11, 12, 14, 16 20 A version change with a rationale and a responsibility, each version in its own file O5 15 10 A 5-minute presentation that justifies two design choices against the options rejected O6 All 15

Track techniques (20 points). Score only the rows for your track. Each track's points add up to 20. Give half the points when a technique is there but incomplete, for example a derived variable that lists one of its two sources.

Technique Module Full points when A B C D Questionnaire flow 10 An Instrument points at a main Sequence, and an IfThenElse gate routes at least one section - - - 10 Lineage 11 Every derived variable lists all its source variables in source_variable_references 20 10 - - Linkage 12 Both sources are studies in one document, the key is tagged on both sides, a Comparison maps the keys, and the method is recorded - 10 - - Custom fields 14 Every key comes from a written catalog with one namespace, and an audit counts the items that carry them - - 20 - Specification 16 The spec passes ddi spec validate, its gates match the instrument's (equivalent()), and the plan says what each gate does with a missing answer - - - 10

Scoring guide:

  • 90-100: Excellent. You can take data from a file to a valid, versioned DDI document, record what your track needs, and explain your choices. The rubric checks these skills on one dataset; it does not test every part of ddi-l.
  • 70-89: Good. For each row where you lost points, review the modules listed beside it.
  • 50-69: Needs practice. Redo the exercises of the modules beside your weakest rows, and try again.
  • Below 50: Start with Track A and work through the steps slowly.

items.title: Reflection questions
items.text:
These are open-ended questions. There are no right or wrong answers. Write your thoughts in a notebook or discuss with your group.

  1. What was the hardest part of building your DDI document? What would you do differently next time?

  2. How would you explain DDI to a colleague who has never heard of it? Try to describe it in two or three simple sentences.

  3. Which part of the ddi-l API did you use the most? Why? Think about which methods you called again and again, and what that tells you about your workflow.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can write a plan that gives every column of my dataset its question (or the reason it has none), its type and its code list, and names the techniques my track needs. (O1)
  • I can build the DDI document from the data, with each asked column linked to its question, code lists with categories, concepts and a universe. (O2)
  • I can get no errors from doc.validate(), doc.lint() and ddi validate on every file I save. (O3)
  • I can record the flow, lineage, linkage, custom fields or specification my track needs, and show where it is in the XML. (O4)
  • I can version a change with a rationale and a responsibility, and keep each version in its own file. (O5)
  • I can present my project in 5 minutes and justify two design choices against the options I rejected. (O6)

Instructor notes

  • Let learners choose their track. Self-selection increases engagement. If the group is mixed (students, researchers, archivists, NSO staff), encourage small groups by role.
  • Plan first. Ask to see each plan before learners write code. Ten minutes on the plan saves half an hour of rework.
  • Time management. Track A takes about 60 minutes. Tracks B and D can take 90 minutes or more, because they record two techniques each. Set expectations at the start and let faster learners help slower ones.
  • Peer review. After learners finish, pair them up to review each other's deliverables. Each reviewer should run ddi validate on the other person's files and score them with the rubric.
  • Show-and-tell. End with the presentations: 2-3 learners share their screen and follow the five parts of "Present your project". Focus on the design choices, not just what they built.
  • Common issues: Learners often forget to link variables to questions, skip the version rationale, or append a second rationale to a study that already has one (a version holds one rationale, and the file fails validation). The checklist helps catch these gaps.
  • Extension: Advanced learners can try a second track or combine elements from two tracks (for example, Track B's linkage with Track D's validation script).
  • Celebration. This is the last core module. Acknowledge the effort learners have put in. Hand out certificates or badges if your organization supports them. Point those who use the logic or server extra to the optional Modules 18 and 19.

items.title: Module 18 (optional): Decide gates exactly
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Check whether two gates hold for the same respondents with decide(), and read its verdict: equivalent, different with a respondent who tells them apart, or unknown with a reason.
  • O2. Give decide() the type of each question, taken from the spec's response domains, and explain why a whole-number question can make two gates agree.
  • O3. Test a gate with evaluate() on respondents you choose: one who left the question empty, one who refused it, one who answered without a value, and one who gave a value.
  • O4. Review gates translated from a specification document, and name for each one that differs from the intended gate a respondent it routes wrongly.
  • O5. Say what the logic extra changes in equivalent() and ddi conform, and what they do without it.

Prerequisites: Module 16. This module is optional: the capstone does not need it.

Install the spec and logic extras first

This module needs the spec extra of Module 16 and the logic extra, which adds the Z3 solver (about 57 MB). pip install ddi-l alone installs neither:

pip install -U "ddi-l[spec,logic]"

Time: 45 min self-paced / 60 min instructor-led.

New in this module: decide(), its verdict (outcome, example, reason), Example.describe(), evaluate(), Answer, the types argument, equivalent(exact=...) and ddi conform --semantics.

items.title: 1. What a normal form cannot tell you
items.text:
In Module 16, normalise() put each gate in a normal form, and equivalent() compared those forms. A normal form spells things out and moves not inward, but it calculates nothing. So two gates that always agree can still have different normal forms:

from ddi_l.spec import equivalent

print(equivalent("PetCount > 0", "PetCount >= 1", exact=False))  # -> False

exact=False asks for the normal forms only, which is all equivalent() does without the logic extra. False then means only "written differently". It does not mean that some household is routed differently.

The logic extra adds a solver: a program that searches every possible respondent for one that two gates disagree on. When it finds none, the gates are equivalent. When it finds one, it shows you that respondent.

items.title: 2. Check that the extra is installed
items.text:
decide() asks the solver. Without the extra it raises LogicDependencyError, which says what to install:

from ddi_l.spec import LogicDependencyError, decide

try:
    print(decide("x > 3", "x >= 4").outcome)  # -> different
except LogicDependencyError as error:
    print(error)

If you see different, the extra works. If you see Deciding expressions needs z3-solver: pip install "ddi-l[logic]", run that command.

items.title: 3. Three verdicts
items.text:
decide(left, right) returns a verdict with three parts:

Part What it holds outcome "equivalent", "different" or "unknown" example For different: a respondent one gate holds for and the other does not reason For unknown: why the solver could not decide 
same = decide("PetAge + 1 > 11", "PetAge > 10")
print(same.outcome)  # -> equivalent

apart = decide("answered(PetKind) and PetAge > 30", "PetAge > 30")
print(apart.outcome)  # -> different
print(apart.example.describe())  # -> PetAge is 31 and PetKind is empty

unsure = decide('PetName = "Rex"', 'PetName < "S"')
print(unsure.outcome)  # -> unknown
print(unsure.reason)  # -> PetName < "S" compares text by order
  • The first pair does arithmetic: PetAge + 1 > 11 holds exactly when PetAge > 10 does. Normalising could not see that; the solver can.
  • The second pair differs for a pet aged 31 whose kind was left empty. Only the first gate needs an answer to PetKind.
  • The third pair compares text by alphabetical order, which the solver does not model. unknown is honest: check such a gate by hand.

describe() puts the respondent in words. A question it does not name was left empty, unless the sentence says otherwise.

One respondent is enough

A different verdict gives one respondent, not all of them. Fix the gate, then run decide() again: it may find another. Another version of the solver may also pick another respondent than the ones printed here; any respondent it gives is one the two gates disagree on.

items.title: 4. Who is a respondent?
items.text:
The solver tries every kind of respondent. For each question, a respondent can:

A respondent... In describe() A comparison such as PetAge > 10 left it empty PetAge is empty is false refused it PetAge is refused is false answered without a value, such as "don't know" PetAge is answered with no value is false gave a value PetAge is 12 compares the value gave several values (a question compared only with = and !=) PetKind is 1 and 2 PetKind = 1 holds if 1 is among them

missing(x) means empty or refused. An answer without a value is answered, so it is not missing. That third row is the one people forget. Module 16 called these two gates for Q6 almost the same:

verdict = decide("not PetAge > 10", "PetAge <= 10 or missing(PetAge)")
print(verdict.outcome)  # -> different
print(verdict.example.describe())  # -> PetAge is answered with no value

A respondent who answers "don't know" sees Q6 with the first gate and skips it with the second. Both may be what a survey wants; the solver makes you choose on purpose.

items.title: 5. Tell the solver what each question is
items.text:
Unless told otherwise, the solver lets a number be a fraction:

verdict = decide("PetCount > 0", "PetCount >= 1")
print(verdict.example.describe())  # -> PetCount is 0.25

No household has a quarter of a pet. The spec says so: PetCount has decimals: 0. The types argument passes that on. It maps each name to numeric, integer, date, text or code:

print(decide("PetCount > 0", "PetCount >= 1", types={"PetCount": "integer"}).outcome)
# -> equivalent

Rather than type each type by hand, read them from the spec. This function does what ddi conform does with the spec's response domains:

from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.spec import example_spec, load_spec

Path("pet-survey.spec.yaml").write_text(example_spec(), encoding="utf-8")
spec = load_spec("pet-survey.spec.yaml")


def spec_types(spec):
    """What the spec says each question is, as decide() takes it."""
    types = {}
    for question in spec.questions:
        domain = question.domain
        if domain is None:
            continue
        if domain.kind == "numeric":
            types[question.id] = "integer" if domain.decimals == 0 else "numeric"
        else:
            types[question.id] = domain.kind
    return types


types = spec_types(spec)
print(types["PetCount"], types["PetKind"], types["VisitDate"])  # -> integer code date

With the extra, equivalent() uses the solver too, and takes the same types:

print(equivalent("PetCount > 0", "PetCount >= 1", types=types))  # -> True

items.title: 6. Test a gate on respondents you choose
items.text:
decide() searches for a respondent. evaluate() does the opposite: you give it one respondent, and it says whether a gate holds for them. A respondent is a dictionary from question names to Answer objects. An Answer has a state ("empty", "refused" or "answered") and, when answered, a set of values. Numbers are Fractions, so that 0.1 stays exact:

from fractions import Fraction

from ddi_l.spec import Answer, evaluate

respondents = {
    "left it empty": {},
    "refused": {"PetAge": Answer("refused")},
    "did not know": {"PetAge": Answer("answered")},
    "aged 8": {"PetAge": Answer("answered", frozenset({Fraction(8)}))},
    "aged 12": {"PetAge": Answer("answered", frozenset({Fraction(12)}))},
}
for gate in ("not PetAge > 10", "PetAge <= 10 or missing(PetAge)"):
    print(gate, [evaluate(gate, answers) for answers in respondents.values()])
# -> not PetAge > 10 [True, True, True, True, False]
# -> PetAge <= 10 or missing(PetAge) [True, True, False, True, False]

The two rows differ in one column only, "did not know", as decide() said. A table like this is a test of the gate: write the respondents first, say what the gate should do for each, then check.

A different verdict can be checked the same way: its example holds answers that evaluate() takes. Take the verdict of section 5, without types:

verdict = decide("PetCount > 0", "PetCount >= 1")
print(evaluate("PetCount > 0", verdict.example.answers))  # -> True
print(evaluate("PetCount >= 1", verdict.example.answers))  # -> False

items.title: 7. Review translated gates
items.text:
A colleague translated the "go to" instructions of a specification document into gates. You have the gates the survey owner intends. Check them all in one loop:

intended = {
    "PetName": "answered(PetKind)",
    "VetVisits": "PetAge > 10",
    "Toys": "not PetAge > 10",
}
translated = {
    "PetName": "not empty(PetKind) and not refused(PetKind)",
    "VetVisits": "PetAge >= 11",
    "Toys": "PetAge <= 10",
}
for question, gate in intended.items():
    verdict = decide(gate, translated[question], types=types)
    if verdict.outcome == "different":
        print(f"{question}: differs when {verdict.example.describe()}")
    else:
        print(f"{question}: {verdict.outcome}")
# -> PetName: equivalent
# -> VetVisits: equivalent
# -> Toys: differs when PetAge is answered with no value

Two translations are written differently and are right. One routes a "don't know" past Toys. That is the line to discuss with your colleague, not the other two.

items.title: 8. In ddi conform
items.text:
With the extra installed, ddi conform compares gates and edits as decide() does, once their normal forms differ. It takes the types from the spec's domains, as spec_types() does. So:

  • a gate written differently that always agrees with the spec's is not reported: PetCount >= 1 passes for a spec that says PetCount > 0;
  • a gate that differs names a respondent in its message:
Module pets is gated by PetCount > 1; the spec says PetCount > 0 (they differ when PetCount is 1).

--semantics syntactic compares normal forms only, as without the extra; --semantics smt fails when the extra is not installed. From Python, pass semantics="syntactic" or semantics="smt" to conform().

Without the logic extra With it equivalent() Compares normal forms: False may be a false alarm Decides: False means a respondent is routed differently decide() Raises LogicDependencyError Returns a verdict ddi conform Reports every gate written differently Reports only gates that differ, with a respondent

items.title: 9. Limits
items.text:
• Some comparisons are not modelled. Text compared by order, a name compared both with numbers and with text, and a value used as a condition give unknown. Check those gates by hand.
  • The code list is not read. decide() knows that PetKind is a code, not which codes it has, so a respondent may answer a code your list lacks.
  • A work limit bounds the solver, not a clock, so the same pair of gates gets the same verdict on every run, however busy the machine. A pair too hard to decide within that work is unknown.

Scenario

The Pet survey team is reviewing a new version of the questionnaire. A colleague translated the specification document's jumps into gates, and the build team has changed a few gates "to make them simpler". Before anything goes to the field, you check every changed gate against the spec and list each respondent who would now see different questions.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1. (O1) Predict the verdict of each pair, then check it with decide(). For each different, print the respondent; for each unknown, the reason. (a) missing(PetKind) and empty(PetKind) or refused(PetKind). (b) PetAge > 10 and PetAge * 2 > 20. (c) PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 2 and PetKind != 3. (d) PetName = "Rex" and PetName < "S".

    Expected output:

    equivalent
equivalent
different: PetKind is another value
unknown: PetName < "S" compares text by order
    Answer 
    pairs = [
    ("missing(PetKind)", "empty(PetKind) or refused(PetKind)"),
    ("PetAge > 10", "PetAge * 2 > 20"),
    ("PetKind = 1 or PetKind = 2", "PetKind != 3"),
    ('PetName = "Rex"', 'PetName < "S"'),
]
for left, right in pairs:
    verdict = decide(left, right, types=types)
    if verdict.outcome == "different":
        print(f"different: {verdict.example.describe()}")
    elif verdict.outcome == "unknown":
        print(f"unknown: {verdict.reason}")
    else:
        print(verdict.outcome)

    (a) is the definition of missing(). (b) is arithmetic. (c) differs for a code that neither gate names: the solver does not read the Species list, so for it a fourth code exists. A respondent with two codes, 1 and 3, also tells them apart. (d) compares text by order, which the solver does not model.

  2. (O2) Without types, decide("PetAge > 30", "PetAge >= 31") says different. Print the respondent. Then decide the pair again with the types of the spec, and explain the change.

    Expected output:

    PetAge is 30.25
equivalent
    Answer 
    print(decide("PetAge > 30", "PetAge >= 31").example.describe())  # -> PetAge is 30.25
print(decide("PetAge > 30", "PetAge >= 31", types=types).outcome)  # -> equivalent

    Without types, a pet can be 30.25 years old, which PetAge > 30 accepts and PetAge >= 31 does not. The spec gives PetAge decimals: 0, so spec_types() makes it an integer, and no whole number lies between 30 and 31.

  3. (O3) The spec's edit age_range fires when PetAge > 30. A second edit should fire when the age is missing. Using the respondents of section 6 plus a pet aged 31, print for each respondent whether PetAge > 30 fires, then whether missing(PetAge) fires. Which respondent without a usable age is caught by neither? Write a third edit that catches only that respondent.

    Expected output:

    [False, False, False, False, False, True]
[True, True, False, False, False, False]
[False, False, True, False, False, False]
    Answer 
    aged_31 = {"PetAge": Answer("answered", frozenset({Fraction(31)}))}
everyone = [*respondents.values(), aged_31]
print([evaluate("PetAge > 30", answers) for answers in everyone])
print([evaluate("missing(PetAge)", answers) for answers in everyone])
dont_know = "answered(PetAge) and not (PetAge > 30 or PetAge <= 30)"
print([evaluate(dont_know, answers) for answers in everyone])

    The "did not know" respondent is caught by neither: the answer has no value, so the comparison is false, and it is answered, so it is not missing. The expressions have no word for "don't know", but the third edit says it: the age is answered, yet neither PetAge > 30 nor PetAge <= 30 holds, which happens only when there is no value to compare.

  4. (O4) Module 16's housing survey asks Own (1 Yes, 2 No), then YearsOwned and Mortgage to everyone who does not answer "No", then Refinanced to owners of more than 5 years. A colleague wrote the gates below. Check each against the intended gate, with Own a code and YearsOwned a whole number, and print one line per question.

    intended = {
    "YearsOwned": "not Own = 2",
    "Mortgage": "not Own = 2",
    "Refinanced": "YearsOwned > 5",
}
translated = {
    "YearsOwned": "not Own = 2",
    "Mortgage": "Own = 1",
    "Refinanced": "YearsOwned >= 6",
}

    Expected output:

    YearsOwned: equivalent
Mortgage: differs when Own is answered with no value
Refinanced: equivalent
    Answer 
    housing = {"Own": "code", "YearsOwned": "integer"}
for question, gate in intended.items():
    verdict = decide(gate, translated[question], types=housing)
    if verdict.outcome == "different":
        print(f"{question}: differs when {verdict.example.describe()}")
    else:
        print(f"{question}: {verdict.outcome}")

    Mortgage is the one to raise. With Own = 1, a respondent who answers "don't know" to Own, or leaves it empty or refuses it, skips the mortgage question but still sees YearsOwned. Either both questions use not Own = 2, or the survey owner decides they are for home owners only and both use Own = 1. The two gates written differently for Refinanced agree for every whole number of years.

  5. (O1, O3) Show that a different verdict is right: decide not PetAge > 10 against PetAge <= 10, then evaluate both gates on the verdict's respondent.

    Expected output:

    True
False
    Answer 
    verdict = decide("not PetAge > 10", "PetAge <= 10", types=types)
print(evaluate("not PetAge > 10", verdict.example.answers))  # -> True
print(evaluate("PetAge <= 10", verdict.example.answers))  # -> False

    Whatever respondent the solver gives (an empty, refused or "don't know" age), one gate holds and the other does not. ddi-l makes the same check on every different verdict before it reports one.

  6. (O5) With the logic extra, ddi conform reports: Module pets is gated by PetCount > 1; the spec says PetCount > 0 (they differ when PetCount is 1). (a) Who is routed wrongly, and which side do you fix? (b) The instrument had PetCount >= 1 instead. What does ddi conform report with the extra, and what without it?

    Answer

    (a) A household with exactly one pet skips the pets module, though the spec asks it about its pet. The spec is the record, so fix the instrument's gate, unless the survey owner says that one-pet households were meant to skip it; then fix the spec and give it a new version.

    (b) With the extra, nothing: the spec says PetCount is a whole number, and for whole numbers PetCount >= 1 and PetCount > 0 agree. Without it, spec.gate.different, because the normal forms differ. That finding is a false alarm, which is why the report shows both normal forms.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): decide() returns different. What do you know?

A. The two gates are written differently.

B. At least one respondent sees the item with one gate and not with the other, and example holds one.

C. Every respondent is routed differently.

D. The gates use different questions.

Answer

B. A different verdict comes with one respondent the gates disagree on. A is true but says less: gates written differently can still be equivalent. C and D do not follow.

Question 2 (O3): A respondent answers PetAge with “don't know”. Is missing(PetAge) true?

A. Yes: there is no age.

B. No: the question is answered, without a value, and missing() means empty or refused.

C. Only with the logic extra.

D. Only if PetAge is an integer.

Answer

B. missing(x) is empty(x) or refused(x). An answer without a value is neither, and any comparison of it is false.

Question 3 (O2): Why does decide() say PetCount > 0 and PetCount >= 1 differ, until you pass types?

A. Because the solver has a bug with >=.

B. Because without types a number may be a fraction, such as 0.25, which the first gate accepts and the second does not.

C. Because PetCount might be text.

D. Because one of them reads an empty answer as 0.

Answer

B. types={"PetCount": "integer"}, which spec_types() reads from decimals: 0, rules out fractions, and the two agree.

Question 4 (O1): decide() returns unknown. What do you do?

A. Treat the gates as equivalent.

B. Treat them as different.

C. Read reason, and check that pair of gates by hand or rewrite it in a form the solver models.

D. Run it again until it decides.

Answer

C. unknown means the solver could not decide, for the reason given. The verdict is the same on every run, so D does not help.

Question 5 (O5): Without the logic extra, ddi conform reports spec.gate.different for a gate. What can you conclude?

A. Some respondent is routed differently.

B. The normal forms differ. The gates may still always agree, so compare the two normal forms in the report, or install the extra and run it again.

C. The instrument is invalid DDI.

D. The spec is wrong.

Answer

B. Without the extra nothing is calculated: PetCount >= 1 against PetCount > 0 is reported, though no household is routed differently.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can check two gates with decide() and read its verdict, its respondent or its reason. (O1)
  • I can read each question's type from the spec and pass it as types, and explain why a whole number changes the verdict. (O2)
  • I can test a gate with evaluate() on an empty, a refused, a "don't know" and an answered question. (O3)
  • I can review translated gates and name a respondent each wrong one routes differently. (O4)
  • I can say what the logic extra changes in equivalent() and ddi conform. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start from Module 16's two gates for Q6 (section 4). Ask the room whether they are the same before you run decide(). Most say yes.
  • The "answered with no value" row of section 4 surprises everyone. Ask for a real question where "don't know" should see the follow-up, and one where it should not.
  • Section 6 is a habit worth more than the solver: write the respondents and the expected result before checking a gate. Testers do the same.
  • If Z3 cannot be installed on the training machines, section 1 and the first example of section 6 still work: equivalent(exact=False) and evaluate() need no solver. Run the rest on the projector.

See also: Module 16: Advanced questionnaire specification | Check a questionnaire against a spec

items.title: Module 19 (optional): Serve ddi-l over HTTP
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Start the service with ddi serve, check that it runs with /health, and find an endpoint's query parameters in the interactive documentation at /schema.
  • O2. Validate and lint a document over HTTP, from the shell and from Python, and read valid, schema_issues and lint_findings in the answer.
  • O3. Convert a document to JSON and back over HTTP, and check that the round trip kept every byte.
  • O4. Tell from a status code and its detail what was wrong with a request (400, 405, 413, 503 or 504), and fix the request.
  • O5. Choose the settings of a shared deployment (address, largest document, origins allowed, interactive documentation) and build the service with create_app(ServerConfig(...)).

Prerequisites: Module 7. This module is optional: the capstone does not need it.

Install the server extra first

The service needs the server extra, which adds Litestar (the web framework) and uvicorn (the program that serves it). pip install ddi-l alone installs neither:

pip install -U "ddi-l[server]"

Time: 45 min self-paced / 60 min instructor-led.

New in this module: ddi serve, /health, /schema, POST /v1/validate, POST /v1/lint, POST /v1/convert/json, POST /v1/convert/xml, create_app(), ServerConfig, Litestar's TestClient.

items.title: 1. Why a service?
items.text:
In Module 7 you ran ddi validate and ddi lint on your own machine. Other people and programs may need the same checks: a deposit form on a website, a pipeline written in Java or R, a CI job in another language. They cannot all install Python and ddi-l.

A service answers requests sent over HTTP, the protocol of the web. You run ddi-l once, as a service, and every program that can send an HTTP request can validate a document. The service calls the same code as the ddi command, so both give the same answer for the same document.

Each request goes to an endpoint: a path such as /v1/validate, with a method. GET asks for something; POST sends something, here a document, in the request's body. The service answers with a status code (200 means it worked) and, here, a JSON body.

items.title: 2. Start the service
items.text:
In a terminal:

ddi serve

Interactive API docs: http://localhost:8000/schema
OpenAPI document:     http://localhost:8000/schema/openapi.json
INFO:     Started server process [1550]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)

The service now listens on port 8000 of this machine only (127.0.0.1), until you press Ctrl+C. Leave this terminal open and open a second one for the commands below.

Port 8000 already in use?

If ddi serve stops with "address already in use" (on Windows: "only one usage of each socket address ... is normally permitted"), another program already listens on port 8000: mkdocs serve does by default, for one. Start the service on another port with ddi serve --port 8001, and use 8001 instead of 8000 in this module's addresses. An answer that is a web page saying "404 - Not found" means a command still went to port 8000, to the other program.

Check that it answers, from the second terminal:

Windows PowerShellmacOS and Linux 
Invoke-RestMethod http://localhost:8000/health

curl http://localhost:8000/health

{"status":"ok","version":"X.Y.Z"}

PowerShell shows the same two fields as a small table. In place of X.Y.Z you see the version of ddi-l you installed.

Windows PowerShell has its own curl

In Windows PowerShell, curl is another command, and @ means something else, so the macOS and Linux commands fail there (The splatting operator '@' cannot be used...). Use the Windows PowerShell tab, or type curl.exe and put the file name in quotes: curl.exe --data-binary "@pets.xml" http://localhost:8000/v1/validate.

Now open http://localhost:8000/schema in a browser. This is the interactive documentation: every endpoint, what to send, its query parameters (the ?name=value part of an address) and what comes back, with examples. Open POST /v1/validate, press Try it out, then Execute: the body is filled in with a valid document, and you get a real answer. /schema/fr shows the same page with the descriptions in French.

items.title: 3. Validate and lint
items.text:
Save a small document to send:

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.new_study(title="Pet Survey", agency="example.org")
doc.add_question(text="How many pets live here?")
doc.add_variable(name="PetCount")
doc.save("pets.xml")

Send it to /v1/validate from the second terminal:

Windows PowerShellmacOS and Linux 
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://localhost:8000/v1/validate `
  -InFile pets.xml -ContentType application/xml | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

curl --data-binary @pets.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/validate

--data-binary @pets.xml and -InFile pets.xml both send the file as the body, byte for byte. The answer has four fields:

Field What it holds valid true when the document has no error, from the schema or from lint schema_issues Each schema error: message, line, xpath, context lint_findings Each lint finding: rule_id, severity, message, location messages All of them in one list, each marked with its source

Warnings do not make a document invalid, just as ddi lint returns 0 when it reports only warnings.

items.title: The same request from Python
items.text:
To try the service from Python, you do not need to start it. Litestar, which the server extra installs, has a test client that sends requests to the service inside your own program. It is also how you would test a deployment's settings:

import logging
from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.server import create_app
from litestar.testing import TestClient

# The test client logs every request; keep the output to what you print.
logging.getLogger("httpx").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

client = TestClient(app=create_app())
xml = Path("pets.xml").read_bytes()

response = client.post("/v1/validate", content=xml)
print(response.status_code)  # -> 200
report = response.json()
print(report["valid"], len(report["schema_issues"]))  # -> True 0
for finding in report["lint_findings"]:
    print(finding["severity"], finding["rule_id"])
# -> warning ddi.maintainable.labels

The question and the variable have no label, hence two warnings. The document is still valid.

client.post() and client.get() take the same paths, query parameters and bodies as curl, so everything below works on a running service too.

items.title: Query parameters
items.text:
The options of ddi lint travel as query parameters:

Parameter On Does lint=false /v1/validate Schema validation only version=3.2 every document endpoint Validate against that DDI version, not the one the document declares rule=... /v1/lint Run only that rule (repeat it for several) skip_rule=... /v1/lint Leave out that rule's findings profile=... /v1/lint Run a lint profile lint_config=... /v1/lint, /v1/validate The JSON that ddi lint --lint-config reads 
quiet = client.post(
    "/v1/lint", params={"skip_rule": "ddi.maintainable.labels"}, content=xml
)
print(quiet.json())  # -> {'lint_findings': []}

From the shell, put them in the address, in quotes, because & and ? mean something to the shell:

Windows PowerShellmacOS and Linux 
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -InFile pets.xml -ContentType application/xml `
  -Uri "http://localhost:8000/v1/lint?skip_rule=ddi.maintainable.labels"

curl --data-binary @pets.xml 'http://localhost:8000/v1/lint?skip_rule=ddi.maintainable.labels'

items.title: 4. Convert to JSON and back
items.text:
/v1/convert/json turns a document into JSON, as ddi to-json does, and /v1/convert/xml turns that JSON back into XML:

as_json = client.post("/v1/convert/json", content=xml)
print(as_json.headers["content-type"])  # -> application/json
back = client.post(
    "/v1/convert/xml",
    content=as_json.content,
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
)
print(back.content == xml)  # -> True

The round trip gave back the same bytes. Send JSON with the header Content-Type: application/json, so the service reads the body as JSON:

Windows PowerShellmacOS and Linux 
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/json `
  -InFile pets.xml -ContentType application/xml -OutFile pets.json
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/xml `
  -InFile pets.json -ContentType application/json -OutFile pets-back.xml

curl --data-binary @pets.xml http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/json -o pets.json
curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @pets.json \
  http://localhost:8000/v1/convert/xml -o pets-back.xml

-o and -OutFile save the answer to a file, with its bytes as sent.

items.title: 5. When a request fails
items.text:
A status code of 400 or more means the request did not work. The body says why, in detail:

answer = client.post("/v1/validate", params={"version": "4.0"}, content=xml)
print(answer.status_code, answer.json()["detail"])
# -> 400 Unsupported DDI schema version: '4.0'
Code Means Fix 400 Bad Request The body or a parameter cannot be read: not XML, not JSON, an unknown version Send the file itself, with --data-binary, and check the parameter 405 Method Not Allowed The wrong method, such as GET on /v1/validate Use POST for the endpoints that take a document 413 Request Entity Too Large The body is larger than the service accepts (32 MB by default) Send a smaller file, or raise the limit when you start the service 422 Unprocessable Content Metadata tables were read but have problems (/v1/tables/import) Fix the rows listed in extra 503 Service Unavailable The service is already working on as many documents as it may Wait the seconds in the Retry-After header and send it again 504 Gateway Timeout The answer took longer than 60 seconds Send a smaller document, or ask whoever runs the service

A document that is not valid DDI is not an error: the answer is 200, with valid false and the schema errors listed. 400 means the service could not read what you sent at all.

items.title: 6. Run it for other people
items.text:
ddi serve alone listens on this machine only, which is what you want while you learn. To serve other machines, the person who runs the service chooses its settings:

Setting ddi serve option ServerConfig field Default Address to listen on --host 0.0.0.0 (all of this machine's networks) (set by the server program) 127.0.0.1 Largest body --max-body-mb max_body_bytes 32 MiB Documents at once --max-jobs max_concurrent_jobs the number of CPUs Websites whose pages may call it --cors-allow-origin (repeat it) cors_allow_origins none Interactive documentation --no-openapi turns it off enable_openapi on

CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) is how a browser decides whether a web page from one site may call a service on another. Name each site that needs it; there is no "allow every site" option, on purpose.

For a real deployment, build the service in a Python file, here myapp.py, and run it with uvicorn, which can start several worker processes:

from ddi_l.server import ServerConfig, create_app

app = create_app(
    ServerConfig(
        max_body_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024,
        cors_allow_origins=("https://deposit.example.org",),
        enable_openapi=False,
    )
)

Run this from the folder that holds myapp.py. myapp:app names the file (without .py) and the variable in it, so use your own file's name if it differs:

uvicorn myapp:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4

The service reads XML with the same protections as the library: no entities, no network access, nothing written to disk. Validation keeps a processor busy, so put the service behind a proxy that limits how many requests each caller sends, and size it for your largest document. The HTTP API guide has the details.

Scenario

Your data archive builds a deposit form on its website. When a researcher uploads a DDI file, the form must say at once whether it is valid, and list the problems. The web team writes JavaScript, not Python. You run ddi-l as a service for them, show them which requests to send and what the answers mean, and choose its settings.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1. (O1) Start ddi serve and check /health. Then, in the interactive documentation, find the query parameters that POST /v1/lint takes. Check your list from Python by asking the test client for /v1/versions, then for the OpenAPI document at /schema/openapi.json.

    Expected output:

    {'default': '3.3', 'supported': ['3.1', '3.2', '3.3']}
['version', 'profile', 'rule', 'skip_rule', 'lint_config']
    Answer 
    print(client.get("/v1/versions").json())
openapi = client.get("/schema/openapi.json").json()
lint = openapi["paths"]["/v1/lint"]["post"]
print([parameter["name"] for parameter in lint["parameters"]])

    /v1/versions lists the DDI versions the service validates against, and the one it uses when a document does not say. The OpenAPI document is what the interactive documentation is drawn from, so its list matches what you found in the browser.

  2. (O2) Lint pets.xml over HTTP with an allowed-agency list that does not hold example.org, using lint_config. Print each finding's rule. Then send the same lint_config to /v1/validate and print valid.

    Expected output:

    ['ddi.agency.allowed', 'ddi.maintainable.labels', 'ddi.maintainable.labels']
True
    Answer 
    config = '{"allowed_agencies": ["ca.statcan"]}'
found = client.post("/v1/lint", params={"lint_config": config}, content=xml)
print([finding["rule_id"] for finding in found.json()["lint_findings"]])
checked = client.post("/v1/validate", params={"lint_config": config}, content=xml)
print(checked.json()["valid"])

    ddi.agency.allowed reports the agency example.org, which the list does not allow. It is a warning, like the two missing labels, so the document is still valid. The configuration applies to this request only: the next request without it gets the default checks.

  3. (O2) Break pets.xml as in Module 7: change <r:Version>1</r:Version> to <r:Version>one</r:Version>. Send it to /v1/validate and print the status code, valid, and the line and message of the schema error.

    Expected output:

    200 False
5 value doesn't match any pattern of ['[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)*']
    Answer 
    broken = xml.replace(b"<r:Version>1</r:Version>", b"<r:Version>one</r:Version>", 1)
answer = client.post("/v1/validate", content=broken)
report = answer.json()
print(answer.status_code, report["valid"])
issue = report["schema_issues"][0]
print(issue["line"], issue["message"])

    The status code is 200: the service read the document and did its job. The document is what is wrong, so valid is false and the error says where.

  4. (O3) Convert pets.xml to JSON over HTTP and back again. Is the XML that comes back the same as the file, byte for byte?

    Expected output:

    True
    Answer 
    as_json = client.post("/v1/convert/json", content=xml)
back = client.post(
    "/v1/convert/xml",
    content=as_json.content,
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
)
print(back.content == xml)

    The JSON keeps everything the XML holds, so the round trip is exact. Its keys carry each element's namespace in braces, as in ddi to-json: look at as_json.json() to see them.

  5. (O4) For each failed request, say what is wrong and how to fix it. (a) GET /v1/validate gives 405. (b) POST /v1/validate?version=3.4 gives 400. (c) A 50 MB file gives 413 from a service started with ddi serve. (d) A request gives 503 at a busy hour.

    Answer

    (a) /v1/validate takes a document, so it needs POST with the document as the body. (b) The service knows DDI 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 (see /v1/versions): drop version or pick one of those. (c) The default limit is 32 MB: whoever runs the service raises it, for example ddi serve --max-body-mb 64.
