(d) The service is working on as many documents as it may: wait the seconds in Retry-After and send it again. A client written for a service should do this on its own.

  6. (O5) The deposit form of the scenario runs at https://deposit.example.org. Deposits can reach 100 MB. The archive does not want the interactive documentation on the internet. Build the service with create_app(ServerConfig(...)), then check with a test client that /schema is gone and that a deposit-form page may call /v1/validate. Write the ddi serve command with the same settings.

    Expected output:

    404
https://deposit.example.org
    Answer 
    from ddi_l.server import ServerConfig

deposit = create_app(
    ServerConfig(
        max_body_bytes=100 * 1024 * 1024,
        cors_allow_origins=("https://deposit.example.org",),
        enable_openapi=False,
    )
)
checker = TestClient(app=deposit)
print(checker.get("/schema").status_code)
preflight = checker.options(
    "/v1/validate",
    headers={
        "Origin": "https://deposit.example.org",
        "Access-Control-Request-Method": "POST",
    },
)
print(preflight.headers["access-control-allow-origin"])

    A browser asks the service first (this OPTIONS request is the "preflight") and sends the deposit only when the answer names the form's site. The command with the same settings:

    ddi serve --host 0.0.0.0 --max-body-mb 100 --cors-allow-origin https://deposit.example.org --no-openapi

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): You start ddi serve on your laptop. A colleague on another machine cannot reach it. Why?

A. The service needs a password.

B. By default it listens on 127.0.0.1, this machine only. Start it with --host 0.0.0.0 to accept other machines.

C. Port 8000 is reserved for browsers.

D. The colleague must install ddi-l first.

Answer

B. The default keeps a service you are trying out private to your machine.

Question 2 (O2): /v1/validate answers 200 with valid false. What does it mean?

A. The service failed.

B. The request was wrong.

C. The service read the document, and the document has at least one error, listed in schema_issues or lint_findings.

D. The document has warnings.

Answer

C. 200 says the request worked. valid is about the document, and only errors make it false.

Question 3 (O4): Which status code says that the service could not read the body at all?

A. 200

B. 400

C. 413

D. 503

Answer

B. 400 Bad Request: not XML, not JSON, or a parameter it does not know. 413 means the body was too large to read.

Question 4 (O3): Which header do you send with a JSON body to /v1/convert/xml?

A. Accept: application/xml

B. Content-Type: application/json

C. Content-Length: json

D. None: the service guesses.

Answer

B. Content-Type says what the body is. Without it, the service cannot tell JSON from anything else.

Question 5 (O5): A web page on the site forms.example.org must call the service from the browser. What do you set?

A. --cors-allow-origin https://forms.example.org

B. --cors-allow-origin '*'

C. --no-openapi

D. --max-jobs 1

Answer

A. Name each site that may call the service. There is no wildcard, so that a deployment never opens to every site by mistake.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can start ddi serve, check /health, and find an endpoint's query parameters at /schema. (O1)
  • I can validate and lint a document over HTTP and read valid, schema_issues and lint_findings. (O2)
  • I can convert a document to JSON and back over HTTP and check that nothing was lost. (O3)
  • I can tell from a status code and its detail what was wrong with a request, and fix it. (O4)
  • I can choose the settings of a shared deployment and build it with create_app(ServerConfig(...)). (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start the service on the projector and do section 2 live: /health, then Try it out in /schema. Seeing a real answer in the browser makes the rest concrete.
  • Windows learners: curl in Windows PowerShell 5.1 is another command with the same name. Use Invoke-RestMethod as shown, or type curl.exe.
  • The most common confusion is between "the request failed" (400 and up) and "the document is not valid" (200 with valid false). Ask the room which one a deposit form should show to the researcher.
  • Exercise 6 is the one to discuss with anyone who will run the service: who may call it, how large a document can be, and whether the documentation pages should be public.

See also: Module 7: Validate from the command line | HTTP API

items.title: Module 20 (optional): From DDI-Codebook to DDI-Lifecycle, built for reuse
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Explain why a DDI-Codebook file cannot share a question, a code list or a universe with another study, and how DDI-Lifecycle lets every wave of a survey refer to the same item.
  • O2. Read DDI-Codebook files, version 2.5 or 2.6, with Python's xml.etree.ElementTree: each study's citation and data files, and each variable's name, label, question and categories.
  • O3. Find what the codebooks repeat (the same question, the same categories, the same universe) and decide when a repeat is the same item and when a change of wording makes it another one.
  • O4. Write the metadata tables so that each repeated item appears once, referred to by every variable that uses it, and load several waves as one series into a schema-valid DDI-Lifecycle file.
  • O5. Carry over what makes the result findable and reusable: each wave's DOI, a licence a program can read, a record of the conversion and a label on every item.

Prerequisites: Module 9 and Module 15. Module 1 covers the FAIR principles this module puts into practice. This module is optional: the capstone does not need it.

Time: 60 min self-paced / 75 min instructor-led.

New in this module: DDI-Codebook files (stdyDscr, fileDscr, dataDscr, var, catgry), xml.etree.ElementTree, load_tables(), to_fragment(), the groups and datasets tables, the studies table's identifier, copyright and license columns, and run_lint().

items.title: 1. One codebook per study, nothing shared
items.text:
Many data archives describe their holdings in DDI-Codebook (DDI-C), the DDI Alliance's first standard; this course teaches DDI-Lifecycle (DDI-L). The difference that matters here is what each lets you share:

DDI-Codebook DDI-Lifecycle One file holds One study, complete in itself Any items, from one study or many A question, a code list Written inside each variable that uses it An item of its own, which variables refer to Identifiers Local to the file, such as ID="V1" A URN, urn:ddi:agency:id:version, that any file can refer to A survey run every year One codebook per year, each repeating the same questions and categories One question and one code list, referred to by every year's variables

A codebook cannot point outside itself, so each wave's codebook copies everything again. Nothing in the files says that PetKind asks the same question in 2022 and in 2023: a person has to compare them. If a category's label is corrected, it has to be corrected in every codebook.

Converting to DDI-Lifecycle one codebook at a time would keep those copies, each with an identifier of its own. This module converts with reuse in mind: it reads every wave first, finds what they repeat, and writes each repeated item once.

ddi-l reads and writes DDI-Lifecycle only. You read the codebooks with Python's standard library, and hand their content to ddi-l through the metadata tables.

items.title: 2. Two waves, two codebooks
items.text:
A made-up survey ran in 2022 and in 2023, and its archive wrote one codebook per wave, in the same layout each year. The function below writes them, so that you can see what changes from one year to the next. Both files are valid against the DDI Alliance's DDI-Codebook 2.5 schema.

from pathlib import Path

VARIABLES = {
    "PetCount": """
    <var ID="V1" name="PetCount" files="F1" dcml="0">
      <labl>Number of pets</labl>
      <qstn>
        <qstnLit>{count_question}</qstnLit>
      </qstn>
      <varFormat type="numeric"/>
    </var>""",
    "PetKind": """
    <var ID="V2" name="PetKind" files="F1">
      <labl>Kind of pet</labl>
      <qstn>
        <qstnLit>What kind of pet do you have?</qstnLit>
      </qstn>{kinds}
      <varFormat type="numeric"/>
    </var>""",
    "SecondPetKind": """
    <var ID="V3" name="SecondPetKind" files="F1">
      <labl>Kind of second pet</labl>
      <qstn>
        <qstnLit>What kind is your second pet?</qstnLit>
      </qstn>{kinds}
      <varFormat type="numeric"/>
    </var>""",
}
KINDS = "".join(
    f"""
      <catgry{' missing="Y"' if value == "9" else ""}>
        <catValu>{value}</catValu>
        <labl>{label}</labl>
      </catgry>"""
    for value, label in [
        ("1", "Dog"),
        ("2", "Cat"),
        ("3", "Other pet"),
        ("9", "Don't know"),
    ]
)


def write_codebook(year, doi, count_question, names):
    """One wave's codebook: the same layout every year, as an archive writes it."""
    variables = "".join(
        VARIABLES[name].format(count_question=count_question, kinds=KINDS)
        for name in names
    )
    Path(f"pets-{year}.xml").write_text(
        f"""<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<codeBook xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_5" version="2.5">
  <stdyDscr>
    <citation>
      <titlStmt>
        <titl>Pet Ownership Survey {year}</titl>
        <IDNo agency="DOI">{doi}</IDNo>
      </titlStmt>
      <rspStmt>
        <AuthEnty>Example Research Institute</AuthEnty>
      </rspStmt>
      <distStmt>
        <distrbtr>Example Data Archive</distrbtr>
        <distDate date="{year}-09-15">15 September {year}</distDate>
      </distStmt>
    </citation>
    <stdyInfo>
      <sumDscr>
        <anlyUnit>Households</anlyUnit>
        <universe>Households with at least one pet</universe>
        <dataKind>Survey data</dataKind>
      </sumDscr>
    </stdyInfo>
    <dataAccs>
      <useStmt>
        <conditions>Free to reuse with attribution (CC BY 4.0).</conditions>
      </useStmt>
    </dataAccs>
  </stdyDscr>
  <fileDscr ID="F1">
    <fileTxt>
      <fileName>pets-{year}.csv</fileName>
    </fileTxt>
  </fileDscr>
  <dataDscr>{variables}
  </dataDscr>
</codeBook>
""",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )


write_codebook(
    2022,
    "10.5072/FK2PETS22",
    "How many pets live in your home?",
    ["PetCount", "PetKind"],
)
write_codebook(
    2023,
    "10.5072/FK2PETS23",
    "How many pets live in your household?",
    ["PetCount", "PetKind", "SecondPetKind"],
)

Open pets-2022.xml and pets-2023.xml side by side. Between the two years:

  • PetKind asks the same question, with the same four categories;
  • PetCount is worded differently: "home" became "household";
  • 2023 adds SecondPetKind, a new question with the same categories as PetKind, copied once more.

The two codebooks hold five questions and three copies of the four categories. 10.5072 is the DOI prefix set aside for tests, so these DOIs resolve nowhere; an archive's codebook carries the study's real DOI.

items.title: 3. Read a codebook
items.text:
Every element of a codebook is in its namespace, ddi:codebook:2_5 for version 2.5 and ddi:codebook:2_6 for 2.6. The function reads it from the root element, so it reads either version, and returns what the conversion needs as plain Python values:

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET


def text(element, path, C):
    """The text at path under element, spaces tidied, or an empty string."""
    found = element.findtext(path, namespaces=C) or ""
    return " ".join(found.split())


def read_codebook(path):
    """What one codebook says: its study, its data files and its variables."""
    root = ET.parse(path).getroot()
    C = {"c": root.tag[1:].split("}")[0]}
    study = root.find("c:stdyDscr", C)
    id_no = study.find("c:citation/c:titlStmt/c:IDNo", C)
    variables = []
    for var in root.iterfind("c:dataDscr/c:var", C):
        categories = tuple(
            (text(c, "c:catValu", C), text(c, "c:labl", C), c.get("missing") == "Y")
            for c in var.iterfind("c:catgry", C)
        )
        variables.append(
            {
                "name": var.get("name"),
                "label": text(var, "c:labl", C),
                "question": text(var, "c:qstn/c:qstnLit", C),
                "file": var.get("files"),
                "format": var.find("c:varFormat", C).get("type"),
                "decimals": var.get("dcml", "0"),
                "categories": categories,
            }
        )
    return {
        "title": text(study, "c:citation/c:titlStmt/c:titl", C),
        "identifier": id_no.text.strip(),
        "identifier_agency": id_no.get("agency"),
        "creator": text(study, "c:citation/c:rspStmt/c:AuthEnty", C),
        "publisher": text(study, "c:citation/c:distStmt/c:distrbtr", C),
        "published": study.find("c:citation/c:distStmt/c:distDate", C).get("date"),
        "analysis_unit": text(study, "c:stdyInfo/c:sumDscr/c:anlyUnit", C),
        "kind_of_data": text(study, "c:stdyInfo/c:sumDscr/c:dataKind", C),
        "universe": text(study, "c:stdyInfo/c:sumDscr/c:universe", C),
        "files": {
            f.get("ID"): text(f, "c:fileTxt/c:fileName", C)
            for f in root.iterfind("c:fileDscr", C)
        },
        "variables": variables,
    }


waves = {year: read_codebook(f"pets-{year}.xml") for year in (2022, 2023)}
for year, wave in waves.items():
    print(year, wave["identifier"], [var["name"] for var in wave["variables"]])

Expected output:

2022 10.5072/FK2PETS22 ['PetCount', 'PetKind']
2023 10.5072/FK2PETS23 ['PetCount', 'PetKind', 'SecondPetKind']

find() returns the first matching element, or None; findtext() its text; iterfind() goes through every match. A variable's categories become a tuple of (value, label, missing), which Python can compare with another variable's in one step.

items.title: 4. Find what the codebooks repeat
items.text:
Group the variables of all waves by what they share: their question, their categories, and their study's universe. Two variables ask the same question when both its wording and its answers match:

def question_key(var):
    """A question: its wording, and its categories or else its number format."""
    return var["question"], var["categories"] or (var["format"], var["decimals"])


def repeats(waves):
    """The questions, code lists and universes of all waves, and who uses each."""
    questions = {}  # (wording, answers) -> the variables that ask it
    code_lists = {}  # categories -> the variables that use them
    universes = {}  # wording -> the waves that cover it
    for year, wave in waves.items():
        universes.setdefault(wave["universe"], []).append(year)
        for var in wave["variables"]:
            where = f"{var['name']} {year}"
            questions.setdefault(question_key(var), []).append(where)
            if var["categories"]:
                code_lists.setdefault(var["categories"], []).append(where)
    return questions, code_lists, universes


questions, code_lists, universes = repeats(waves)
print(len(questions), len(code_lists), len(universes))  # -> 4 1 1
for (wording, _), users in questions.items():
    print(users, wording)
print(list(code_lists.values()))

Expected output:

4 1 1
['PetCount 2022'] How many pets live in your home?
['PetKind 2022', 'PetKind 2023'] What kind of pet do you have?
['PetCount 2023'] How many pets live in your household?
['SecondPetKind 2023'] What kind is your second pet?
[['PetKind 2022', 'PetKind 2023', 'SecondPetKind 2023']]

Five questions in the codebooks are four distinct ones; three copies of the categories are one code list; and both waves cover the same universe.

The answers are part of the question because every variable takes its answers from its question (section 5). Had the 2023 wave added a category to What kind of pet do you have?, the two waves would ask two questions with the same wording, each with its own code list; grouped by wording alone, PetKind 2023 would have been given the 2022 categories.

Comparing wording is a rule a program can apply, but sameness is a decision. The two PetCount wordings differ by one word, so the converter keeps them apart. Whether "home" and "household" count the same pets is for the survey's owner to say. If they do, map one wording to the other before converting (exercise 4); if the change matters a little, Module 15's versions are the way to record it.

items.title: 5. Write each item once
items.text:
Each distinct question, code list and universe gets one row, with an id (Q1, CL1, U1) that every variable using it names. The rest follows the waves:

  • a group of type Series holds the studies;
  • each wave is a study, with its citation;
  • each wave's data file is a dataset of its study;
  • each variable gets one row per wave, and names its dataset, its question and its universe.
def response(var, code_list_ids):
    """The questions columns that say what kind of answer a variable records."""
    if var["categories"]:
        return {"response": "code", "code_list": code_list_ids[var["categories"]]}
    if var["format"] == "numeric":
        decimal = var["decimals"] != "0"
        return {
            "response": "numeric",
            "numeric_type": "Decimal" if decimal else "Integer",
        }
    return {"response": "text"}


def build_tables(waves):
    """The metadata tables of all waves, with each repeated item written once."""
    questions, code_lists, universes = repeats(waves)
    question_ids = {key: f"Q{n}" for n, key in enumerate(questions, 1)}
    code_list_ids = {cats: f"CL{n}" for n, cats in enumerate(code_lists, 1)}
    universe_ids = {wording: f"U{n}" for n, wording in enumerate(universes, 1)}
    variables = [
        (year, var) for year, wave in waves.items() for var in wave["variables"]
    ]

    tables = {
        "settings": [{"setting": "agency", "value": "example.org"}],
        "groups": [
            {
                "id": "PETS",
                "title@en": "Pet Ownership Survey",
                "type": "Series",
                "studies": "|".join(f"PETS{year}" for year in waves),
            }
        ],
        "universes": [
            {"id": uid, "label@en": wording} for wording, uid in universe_ids.items()
        ],
        "code_lists": [],
        "codes": [],
        "questions": [],
        "studies": [],
        "datasets": [],
        "variables": [],
    }
    for categories, list_id in code_list_ids.items():
        first = next(var for _, var in variables if var["categories"] == categories)
        tables["code_lists"].append({"id": list_id, "label@en": first["label"]})
        for value, label, missing in categories:
            tables["codes"].append(
                {
                    "code_list": list_id,
                    "value": value,
                    "label@en": label,
                    "missing": "true" if missing else "",
                }
            )
    for key, question_id in question_ids.items():
        first = next(var for _, var in variables if question_key(var) == key)
        tables["questions"].append(
            {"id": question_id, "text@en": key[0], **response(first, code_list_ids)}
        )
    for year, wave in waves.items():
        tables["studies"].append(
            {
                "id": f"PETS{year}",
                "title@en": wave["title"],
                "identifier": wave["identifier"],
                "identifier_agency": wave["identifier_agency"],
                "creator": wave["creator"],
                "publisher": wave["publisher"],
                "publication_date": wave["published"],
                "analysis_unit": wave["analysis_unit"],
                "kind_of_data": wave["kind_of_data"],
                "universe": universe_ids[wave["universe"]],
            }
        )
        for file_id, file_name in wave["files"].items():
            tables["datasets"].append(
                {
                    "id": f"{file_id}_{year}",
                    "name": file_name,
                    "label@en": f"{wave['title']} data",
                    "file": file_name,
                    "study": f"PETS{year}",
                }
            )
    for year, var in variables:
        tables["variables"].append(
            {
                "id": f"{var['name']}_{year}",
                "name": var["name"],
                "label@en": var["label"],
                "question": question_ids[question_key(var)],
                "dataset": f"{var['file']}_{year}",
                "universe": universe_ids[waves[year]["universe"]],
            }
        )
    return tables


tables = build_tables(waves)
print(len(tables["questions"]), len(tables["codes"]), len(tables["variables"]))
# -> 4 4 5

A variable takes its question's response, so PetKind gets the code list without naming it twice. A codebook says only numeric or character; dcml="0", no decimals, is what makes PetCount a whole number. The codebook's IDNo and its agency go to the identifier and identifier_agency columns, which write the DOI into the study's citation.

items.title: 6. Load and check the reuse
items.text:
Write each table as a CSV file, load the folder, and write one DDI-Lifecycle file for both waves:

import csv

from ddi_l.tables import load_tables


def write_tables(folder, tables):
    """One CSV file per table, with every column any of its rows uses."""
    folder = Path(folder)
    folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for name, rows in tables.items():
        headers = list(dict.fromkeys(key for row in rows for key in row))
        with open(folder / f"{name}.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
            writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=headers)
            writer.writeheader()
            writer.writerows(rows)


write_tables("pets-tables", tables)
loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
fragment = loaded.to_fragment()
print(fragment.validate())  # -> []
fragment.save("pets-lifecycle.xml")

asked_2022 = loaded.get("variables", "PetKind_2022").question_references[0]
asked_2023 = loaded.get("variables", "PetKind_2023").question_references[0]
print(asked_2022.urn == asked_2023.urn)  # -> True
print(fragment.get_top_level_reference().type_of_object)  # -> Group

to_fragment() writes a DDI-Lifecycle FragmentInstance, one fragment per item, with the series as its top-level item. to_study(), which writes one study like the documents of the earlier modules, has no place for a series or for several studies.

PetKind in 2022 and PetKind in 2023 now point to the same question by its URN, and three variables point to the same code list. A third wave would add its study, its data file and its variables, and refer to the same items again. Correcting a category's label is now one change, in one place.

items.title: 7. Findable and reusable
items.text:
Module 1 showed how DDI supports the FAIR principles. A conversion is the moment to carry over, or add, what codebooks often hold loosely:

  • A persistent identifier. Each wave's DOI, from its IDNo, is now in its study's citation as an r:InternationalIdentifier, and every item has a URN. The URNs say example.org, the made-up agency this course uses; a real agency is registered with the DDI Alliance, as Module 3 explains.
  • A licence a program can read. DDI-Codebook 2.5 has no licence element: conditions of use are free text in useStmt. Version 2.6 adds a license element whose URI attribute holds the licence's web address. In DDI-Lifecycle, the license column writes it as dcterms:license in the study's citation. Give it the address, not the name.
  • A label on every item. The codebooks labelled their variables but not their questions, and a label is what a catalogue or a question bank lists. run_lint() runs the checks of ddi lint on a fragment, and finds them.

The licence and the labels go in the tables, so every later conversion keeps them:

from ddi_l.lint import run_lint

print(len(run_lint(fragment)))  # -> 4
for row in tables["studies"]:
    row["license"] = "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/"
for question in tables["questions"]:
    asker = next(v for v in tables["variables"] if v["question"] == question["id"])
    question["label@en"] = asker["label@en"]
write_tables("pets-tables", tables)

The four findings were ddi.maintainable.labels, one per question.

  • A record of the conversion. Record where the metadata came from as each study's version rationale, as in Module 15. The tables give you each item before it is written, so you can add it there. Then check the result and save it:
from ddi_l.models.base import InternationalString, VersionRationale

loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
for year in waves:
    loaded.get("studies", f"PETS{year}").version_rationales.append(
        VersionRationale(
            descriptions=[
                InternationalString(
                    text=f"Converted from the DDI-Codebook 2.5 file pets-{year}.xml."
                )
            ]
        )
    )
fragment = loaded.to_fragment()
print(fragment.validate())  # -> []
print(run_lint(fragment))  # -> []
fragment.save("pets-lifecycle.xml")

items.title: 8. What this conversion leaves out
items.text:
• Reuse beyond questions and code lists. Both PetKind variables could also share a represented variable, which says they record the same thing in the same way: see the represented_variables table of the metadata tables guide.
  • Several languages. A codebook may repeat titl or labl with xml:lang; give each language its column, such as label@fr.
  • Statistics and methodology. A variable's sumStat (frequencies, means) describes the data rather than the study and stays with the archive; method/dataColl maps onto the methodologies table.

Before you convert real codebooks, list the elements they use, and compare the waves before deciding what is the same: tools and teams write DDI-Codebook differently.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1. (O1) A colleague converts each codebook to its own DDI-Lifecycle file, one at a time. Both files are valid. What do they lose compared with the conversion of this module?

    Answer

    Each file gets its own PetKind question and its own code list, with different URNs: nothing says that 2022 and 2023 asked the same question with the same categories, which is exactly what comparing the waves needs. A corrected category label has to be corrected in every file again. Converting all waves together, and writing each repeated item once, keeps that knowledge in the metadata.

  2. (O2) Make a DDI-Codebook 2.6 copy of pets-2023.xml: change the namespace and version, and add a license element as the first child of dataAccs. Read its namespace from the root, and print it with the licence's URI.

    Expected output:

    ddi:codebook:2_6 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
    Answer 
    source = Path("pets-2023.xml").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
source = source.replace(
    'xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_5" version="2.5"',
    'xmlns="ddi:codebook:2_6" version="2.6"',
)
source = source.replace(
    "    <dataAccs>\n",
    "    <dataAccs>\n"
    '      <license URI="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">'
    "CC BY 4.0</license>\n",
)
Path("pets-2023-2.6.xml").write_text(source, encoding="utf-8")

root_26 = ET.parse("pets-2023-2.6.xml").getroot()
C_26 = {"c": root_26.tag[1:].split("}")[0]}
licence = root_26.find("c:stdyDscr/c:dataAccs/c:license", C_26)
print(C_26["c"], licence.get("URI"))
# -> ddi:codebook:2_6 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

    read_codebook() reads this file as it is, because it takes the namespace from the root. A converter can take the licence from license/@URI when a codebook has one, and ask a person when it has only useStmt text.

  3. (O3, O4) The survey runs again in 2024, with the 2023 questionnaire. Write its codebook with write_codebook(), add it to waves, and print the number of distinct questions and code lists, then the number of rows of questions and variables in the rebuilt tables.

    Expected output:

    4 1
4 8
    Answer 
    write_codebook(
    2024,
    "10.5072/FK2PETS24",
    "How many pets live in your household?",
    ["PetCount", "PetKind", "SecondPetKind"],
)
waves[2024] = read_codebook("pets-2024.xml")
questions, code_lists, universes = repeats(waves)
print(len(questions), len(code_lists))  # -> 4 1
tables = build_tables(waves)
print(len(tables["questions"]), len(tables["variables"]))  # -> 4 8

    The third wave adds a study, a data file and three variables, and not one question or code list: its variables refer to the items the first two waves already have.

  4. (O3) The survey's owner decides that "How many pets live in your home?" and "How many pets live in your household?" ask the same thing. Map the 2023 wording to the 2022 one in every wave, rebuild and load the tables, and check that PetCount in 2022 and in 2024 now ask the same question.

    Expected output:

    3
True
    Answer 
    same = {"How many pets live in your household?": "How many pets live in your home?"}
for wave in waves.values():
    for var in wave["variables"]:
        var["question"] = same.get(var["question"], var["question"])
tables = build_tables(waves)
print(len(tables["questions"]))  # -> 3
write_tables("pets-tables", tables)
loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
first = loaded.get("variables", "PetCount_2022").question_references[0]
last = loaded.get("variables", "PetCount_2024").question_references[0]
print(first.urn == last.urn)  # -> True

    The decision is recorded in one place, the same mapping, which the owner can review. The question keeps the 2022 wording; if the 2023 wording should be kept as well, a new version of the question (Module 15) records the change instead.

  5. (O5) Give every variable and question a French label (label@fr), using Nombre d'animaux, Type d'animal and Type du deuxième animal. Load the tables, and print the French label of PetKind_2023 and the number of lint findings.

    Expected output:

    Type d'animal
0
    Answer 
    french = {
    "PetCount": "Nombre d'animaux",
    "PetKind": "Type d'animal",
    "SecondPetKind": "Type du deuxième animal",
}
for variable in tables["variables"]:
    variable["label@fr"] = french[variable["name"]]
for question in tables["questions"]:
    asker = next(v for v in tables["variables"] if v["question"] == question["id"])
    question["label@en"] = asker["label@en"]
    question["label@fr"] = french[asker["name"]]
write_tables("pets-tables", tables)

loaded = load_tables("pets-tables")
labels = loaded.get("variables", "PetKind_2023").labels
print(next(label.text for label in labels if label.lang == "fr"))
# -> Type d'animal
print(len(run_lint(loaded.to_fragment())))  # -> 0

    The column header carries the language, so label@en and label@fr become one label with two strings. Because each question is written once, it is translated once, for every wave.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): Why can two DDI-Codebook files not share PetKind's categories?

A. DDI-Codebook has no categories.

B. A codebook is complete in itself: its identifiers are local to the file, and nothing in it can refer to an item in another file.

C. The categories are in different languages.

D. They can, with catgry.

Answer

B. Each wave's codebook writes the categories again. In DDI-Lifecycle the code list is an item with a URN, which every wave's variables refer to.

Question 2 (O3): The 2022 and 2023 codebooks word one question differently. What does the converter of this module do?

A. It merges them, since the variable has the same name.

B. It keeps two questions, and leaves the decision to merge them to the survey's owner, who can map one wording to the other.

C. It stops with an error.

D. It keeps the most recent wording only.

Answer

B. A variable name is not a question. A program can compare wordings, but whether two wordings ask the same thing is a decision.

Question 3 (O4): In the tables, what ties PetKind_2023 to the 2023 study?

A. Its name.

B. Its dataset column: the 2023 data file, whose study is PETS2023.

C. Its question.

D. The order of the rows.

Answer

B. The question is shared by both waves; the data file belongs to one study, and the variable is a column of that file.

Question 4 (O4): Two waves, three variables with the same four categories. How many code lists does the DDI-Lifecycle file hold?

A. Three.

B. One, which the three variables refer to.

C. Two, one per wave.

D. None: categories stay in the variables.

Answer

B. The categories are compared as a whole, and the same set becomes one code list.

Question 5 (O5): A codebook's conditions of use say “Free to reuse with attribution (CC BY 4.0).” What should the converted file hold?

A. The same sentence, in a custom property.

B. The licence's web address in the citation's dcterms:license, through the license column.

C. Nothing: licences are the archive's business.

D. The word "CC BY 4.0" in the title.

Answer

B. A web address names one licence without ambiguity, and a program can recognize it. The sentence is clear to a person only.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can explain why codebooks repeat questions and categories, and how DDI-Lifecycle lets every wave refer to one item. (O1)
  • I can read DDI-Codebook 2.5 or 2.6 files' citations, files and variables with ElementTree. (O2)
  • I can find the questions, code lists and universes several codebooks repeat, and say when a repeat is the same item. (O3)
  • I can write the tables with each repeated item once, and load several waves as one series. (O4)
  • I can carry over the DOI, add a licence address, a record of the conversion and labels, and check them with the linter. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start with two codebooks of the same survey from the room's own archive, if there are any. Ask learners to find what changed between the years before running any code.
  • The decision in section 4 is the heart of the module: who says that two wordings are the same question? Let the room argue about "home" and "household".
  • Exercise 3 shows the payoff: a third wave adds no question. Run it on the projector.
  • Learners often expect ddi-l to read codebooks itself. It does not, by design: the tables are the documented way in, and they report every problem with its row and column.

See also: Load DDI from spreadsheets | Work with other tools | Module 21: Describe your data with DDI-CDI

items.title: Module 21 (optional): Describe your data with DDI-CDI
items.text:
Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you can:

  • O1. Say what DDI-CDI describes, how it differs from DDI-Lifecycle and DDI-Codebook, and when a project would use it.
  • O2. Map a variable of a ddi-l study onto DDI-CDI: an instance variable whose values come from a substantive value domain, and whose missing values come from a sentinel value domain, each backed by a code list.
  • O3. Describe a data file as a DDI-CDI wide data structure, with an identifier component and measure components, and say how a long structure differs.
  • O4. Write DDI-CDI 1.0 XML from a ddi-l study with Python's xml.etree.ElementTree, and validate it against the DDI Alliance's schema.
  • O5. Explain how DDI-CDI identifies objects and links them, and compare it with a DDI-Lifecycle URN.

Prerequisites: Module 9. Module 20 helps, but is not needed. This module is optional: the capstone does not need it.

Time: 60 min self-paced / 75 min instructor-led.

New in this module: DDI-CDI 1.0, InstanceVariable, SubstantiveValueDomain, SentinelValueDomain, CodeList, Code, Notation, Category, WideDataStructure, IdentifierComponent, MeasureComponent, WideDataSet, xmlschema.XMLSchema11.

items.title: 1. Three DDI standards
items.text:
The DDI Alliance published DDI Cross-Domain Integration (DDI-CDI) 1.0 in January 2025. It does not replace the other two standards; it describes something they do not:

DDI-Codebook DDI-Lifecycle DDI-CDI Describes One study and its data files Studies through their life: concepts, questions, questionnaires, variables, data files Data themselves: each value, in whatever structure it is stored, and the processes that produced it Domains Social sciences Social, economic and health statistics Any domain, so data from different fields can be combined Data structures A data file of rows and columns Record layouts and multidimensional tables Wide, long, multidimensional and key-value Encodings XML XML A UML model, encoded as XML Schema and as an RDF ontology with JSON-LD

A project uses DDI-CDI when it combines data from several sources, such as a survey, a register and sensor readings, and needs to say exactly how each value relates to the others, whatever shape each source has. The survey's own questions and questionnaire stay in DDI-Lifecycle.

ddi-l reads and writes DDI-Lifecycle only. This module reads a ddi-l study and writes the DDI-CDI description of its data with Python's standard library, then checks it against the DDI Alliance's schema.

items.title: 2. The study to describe
items.text:
The study is a data file with one row per household, as in earlier modules: an identifier, the kind of pet, which may be "Don't know", and the number of pets. The metadata tables build it in a few lines:

from pathlib import Path

from ddi_l.tables import load_tables

folder = Path("pets-tables")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
files = {
    "settings": "setting,value\nagency,example.org\n",
    "code_lists": "id,label@en\nPET_KINDS,Kinds of pet\n",
    "codes": (
        "code_list,value,label@en,missing\n"
        "PET_KINDS,1,Dog,\n"
        "PET_KINDS,2,Cat,\n"
        "PET_KINDS,3,Other pet,\n"
        "PET_KINDS,9,Don't know,true\n"
    ),
    "variables": (
        "id,label@en,representation,code_list,numeric_type,max_length\n"
        "HouseholdId,Household identifier,text,,,10\n"
        "PetKind,Kind of pet,code,PET_KINDS,,\n"
        "PetCount,Number of pets,numeric,,Integer,\n"
    ),
}
for name, text in files.items():
    (folder / f"{name}.csv").write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")

tables = load_tables(folder)
items = {item.identifier: item for item in tables.items}
print(len(tables.variables))  # -> 3

items finds any item by its identifier, which is how the code below follows a reference: from a variable to its code list, and from a code to its category.

items.title: 3. Variables in DDI-CDI
items.text:
Both standards describe a variable at three levels, from the most general to the most specific:

Level What it is DDI-Lifecycle DDI-CDI Conceptual What is measured, whatever the answers ConceptualVariable ConceptualVariable Represented What is measured and how the values are recorded RepresentedVariable RepresentedVariable Instance A column of one data file Variable InstanceVariable

In DDI-CDI each level builds on the one above it: an instance variable is a represented variable, which is a conceptual variable. This module writes the instance level only.

The other difference is how values are described. In DDI-Lifecycle, a variable has one code list, and a category is marked isMissing. DDI-CDI splits the values of a variable in two value domains:

  • a substantive value domain: the answers to the question, here Dog, Cat and Other pet;
  • a sentinel value domain: the values that stand for something else, such as "Don't know", "Refused" or "Not applicable".

Each value domain takes its values from a code list. In a code list, a code links a notation, the value stored in the data such as 9, to the category it stands for, such as "Don't know".

items.title: 4. Identify and link objects
items.text:
DDI-CDI identifies an object as DDI-Lifecycle does, by an agency, an identifier and a version, written as three elements of identifier. A link to another object gives the same three parts and the object's class. Four small functions write them:

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

CDI = "http://ddialliance.org/Specification/DDI-CDI/1.0/XMLSchema/"
ET.register_namespace("cdi", CDI)


def cdi(tag, *children, text=None):
    """A cdi: element holding children, or text."""
    element = ET.Element(f"{{{CDI}}}{tag}")
    element.text = text
    element.extend(children)
    return element


def identifier(object_id, agency="example.org", version="1"):
    """What DDI-Lifecycle writes as Agency, ID and Version."""
    return cdi(
        "identifier",
        cdi(
            "ddiIdentifier",
            cdi("dataIdentifier", text=object_id),
            cdi("registrationAuthorityIdentifier", text=agency),
            cdi("versionIdentifier", text=version),
        ),
    )


def link(association, object_id, valid_type, agency="example.org", version="1"):
    """A reference to another object: its identifier and its class."""
    return cdi(
        association,
        cdi(
            "ddiReference",
            cdi("dataIdentifier", text=object_id),
            cdi("registrationAuthorityIdentifier", text=agency),
            cdi("versionIdentifier", text=version),
        ),
        cdi("validType", text=valid_type),
    )


def label(text, language="en"):
    """A label in one language."""
    return cdi(
        "displayLabel",
        cdi(
            "languageSpecificString",
            cdi("content", text=text),
            cdi("language", text=language),
        ),
    )

A link's element is named after the association it stands for: its class, what the link means, and the class it points to. Code_denotes_Category, for example, links a code to the category it denotes. The schema fixes the order of the elements in each class, which these functions follow.

items.title: 5. Code lists and value domains
items.text:
A code list gives three objects per code: the category, the notation and the code that joins them. Each one gets an identifier built from the code list's and the value, so that links between them are easy to write:

def code_list(list_id, codes):
    """A code list, with a Category, a Notation and a Code per code."""
    objects = []
    code_links = []
    for code in codes:
        category = items[code.category.identifier]
        key = f"{list_id}-{code.value}"
        objects.append(
            cdi(
                "Category",
                label(category.labels[0].text),
                identifier(f"category-{key}"),
            )
        )
        objects.append(
            cdi(
                "Notation",
                cdi("content", cdi("content", text=code.value)),
                identifier(f"notation-{key}"),
            )
        )
        objects.append(
            cdi(
                "Code",
                identifier(f"code-{key}"),
                link("Code_denotes_Category", f"category-{key}", "Category"),
                link("Code_uses_Notation", f"notation-{key}", "Notation"),
            )
        )
        code_links.append(link("CodeList_has_Code", f"code-{key}", "Code"))
    listing = cdi(
        "CodeList",
        identifier(list_id),
        cdi("allowsDuplicates", text="false"),
        *code_links,
    )
    return [*objects, listing]

A variable with a code list gets two code lists and two value domains: the substantive codes, and the codes whose category is missing. Then comes the instance variable, with its links to its domains:

def describe(variable):
    """The DDI-CDI objects for one ddi-l variable: its domains and itself."""
    name = variable.names[0].text
    objects = []
    domains = []
    coded = variable.variable_representation.code_representation
    if coded is not None:
        codes = items[coded.code_list_reference.identifier].codes
        missing = [c for c in codes if items[c.category.identifier].isMissing]
        answers = [c for c in codes if c not in missing]
        objects += code_list(f"codes-{name}", answers)
        objects.append(
            cdi(
                "SubstantiveValueDomain",
                identifier(f"values-{name}"),
                link(
                    "SubstantiveValueDomain_takesValuesFrom_EnumerationDomain",
                    f"codes-{name}",
                    "CodeList",
                ),
            )
        )
        if missing:
            objects += code_list(f"missing-{name}", missing)
            objects.append(
                cdi(
                    "SentinelValueDomain",
                    identifier(f"missing-values-{name}"),
                    link(
                        "SentinelValueDomain_takesValuesFrom_EnumerationDomain",
                        f"missing-{name}",
                        "CodeList",
                    ),
                )
            )
            domains.append(
                link(
                    "RepresentedVariable_takesSentinelValuesFrom_SentinelValueDomain",
                    f"missing-values-{name}",
                    "SentinelValueDomain",
                )
            )
        domains.append(
            link(
                "RepresentedVariable_takesSubstantiveValuesFrom_SubstantiveValueDomain",
                f"values-{name}",
                "SubstantiveValueDomain",
            )
        )
    objects.append(
        cdi(
            "InstanceVariable",
            label(variable.labels[0].text),
            identifier(f"variable-{name}"),
            cdi("name", cdi("name", text=name)),
            *domains,
        )
    )
    return objects


model = cdi("DDICDIModels")
for variable in tables.variables:
    model.extend(describe(variable))
print(len(model))  # -> 19

PetKind gives 17 objects: 3 codes of answers and 1 code for "Don't know", with their categories, notations and codes, 2 code lists, 2 value domains and the variable. HouseholdId and PetCount give one instance variable each. All of them sit side by side in DDICDIModels, the root element, and point to each other by identifier.

items.title: 6. The data structure
items.text:
A data file with one row per unit and one column per variable is wide. DDI-CDI describes its structure with one component per column, each defined by its variable:

  • an identifier component for the columns that tell the rows apart, here HouseholdId;
  • a measure component for each column of observed values, here PetKind and PetCount.
components = []
structure_links = []
for variable in tables.variables:
    name = variable.names[0].text
    kind = "IdentifierComponent" if name == "HouseholdId" else "MeasureComponent"
    components.append(
        cdi(
            kind,
            identifier(f"component-{name}"),
            link(
                "DataStructureComponent_isDefinedBy_RepresentedVariable",
                f"variable-{name}",
                "InstanceVariable",
            ),
        )
    )
    structure_links.append(
        link("DataStructure_has_DataStructureComponent", f"component-{name}", kind)
    )

model.extend(components)
model.append(cdi("WideDataStructure", identifier("pets-structure"), *structure_links))
model.append(
    cdi(
        "WideDataSet",
        identifier("pets-data"),
        link(
            "DataSet_isStructuredBy_DataStructure",
            "pets-structure",
            "WideDataStructure",
        ),
    )
)
ET.indent(model)
ET.ElementTree(model).write("pets-cdi.xml", encoding="utf-8", xml_declaration=True)
print(len(model))  # -> 24

The same values could be stored long: one row per household and variable, with a column naming the variable and a column holding its value. DDI-CDI describes that file with a long data structure, in which those two columns are a variable descriptor component and a variable value component. The variables, value domains and code lists stay the same: that is what lets DDI-CDI say that two files hold the same data in different shapes.

items.title: 7. Validate against the schema
items.text:
The DDI Alliance publishes the DDI-CDI 1.0 XML Schema on its DDI-CDI page, and in the release on GitHub. Download it once:

from urllib.request import urlretrieve

urlretrieve(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ddi-cdi/ddi-cdi/v1.0/"
    "build/encoding/xml-schema/ddi-cdi.xsd",
    "ddi-cdi.xsd",
)

Then validate with xmlschema, which pip install ddi-l installs:

import xmlschema

schema = xmlschema.XMLSchema11("ddi-cdi.xsd")
print(schema.is_valid("pets-cdi.xml"))  # -> True
for error in schema.iter_errors("pets-cdi.xml"):
    print(error.path, error.reason)

Use XMLSchema11

The DDI-CDI schema says that it needs an XML Schema 1.1 processor. xmlschema.XMLSchema, the XML Schema 1.0 validator, honours that and skips the whole schema: it then reports that DDICDIModels "is not an element of the schema". xmlschema.XMLSchema11 reads it.

An error names the element where the file departs from the schema. The most common one comes from writing the elements of a class in another order than the schema's.

items.title: 8. What this sketch leaves out
items.text:
DDI-CDI can say much more than this file does:

  • The other levels of each variable. A represented variable shared by several data files, and a conceptual variable with its concept and unit type (households here), would let another file's variables point to the same ones.
  • The values themselves. A data point is one cell of the file, and a datum the value in it. Describing them lets DDI-CDI trace a single value from one file to another.
  • The physical file. How the columns are laid out in a CSV file or a fixed-width file, and the formats of statistical software.
  • The process. Activities and steps record how data were produced or transformed, from collection to the published file.

The DDI Alliance also publishes DDI-CDI as an RDF ontology, with a JSON-LD encoding: the same classes and associations, for linked-data systems.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1. (O1) For each project, which DDI standard fits best? (a) An archive documents a deposited survey file for its catalogue. (b) A statistical agency keeps its questions and code lists in a bank, reused by every wave. (c) A research team combines a survey, hospital records and air-quality readings, and must show how each value was derived.

    Answer

    (a) DDI-Codebook, or DDI-Lifecycle if the archive wants item-level reuse: one study and its file. (b) DDI-Lifecycle: each question and code list is an item with its own identifier and version, referred to by every wave. (c) DDI-CDI: data from different domains and shapes, and the processes that link them. The survey's questionnaire would still be described in DDI-Lifecycle.

  2. (O2, O5) Read pets-cdi.xml back with ElementTree. For each instance variable, print its name and the classes of the value domains it takes values from.

    Expected output:

    HouseholdId []
PetKind ['SentinelValueDomain', 'SubstantiveValueDomain']
PetCount []
    Answer 
    written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for variable in written.iterfind("cdi:InstanceVariable", N):
    name = variable.findtext("cdi:name/cdi:name", namespaces=N)
    domains = [
        valid_type.text for valid_type in variable.iterfind("*/cdi:validType", N)
    ]
    print(name, domains)

    A link holds the class of the object it points to in validType, so a program knows what it will find without following the link. HouseholdId and PetCount have no code list, so this sketch gives them no value domain.

  3. (O3) The same pet data are stored long, with the columns HouseholdId, Variable and Value: Variable holds PetKind or PetCount, and Value the answer. Name the kind of data structure and the component each column gets.

    Answer

    A long data structure (LongDataStructure). HouseholdId is an identifier component, as in the wide file. Variable is a variable descriptor component: its values name the variables, and it is defined by a descriptor variable whose values are PetKind and PetCount. Value is a variable value component: it holds the values of several variables in one column. PetKind and PetCount keep their instance variables and value domains.

  4. (O4) Give every category a French label as well as an English one. Change label() to take several (text, language) pairs, label the categories with Chien, Chat, Autre animal and Ne sait pas, write the file again, and print how many French strings it holds.

    Expected output:

    4
    Answer 
    def label(*strings):
    """A label in each language given, as (text, language) pairs."""
    return cdi(
        "displayLabel",
        *(
            cdi(
                "languageSpecificString",
                cdi("content", text=text),
                cdi("language", text=language),
            )
            for text, language in strings
        ),
    )


french = {"Dog": "Chien", "Cat": "Chat", "Other pet": "Autre animal"}
french["Don't know"] = "Ne sait pas"
written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for category in written.iterfind("cdi:Category", N):
    english = category.findtext(
        "cdi:displayLabel/cdi:languageSpecificString/cdi:content", namespaces=N
    )
    category.remove(category.find("cdi:displayLabel", N))
    category.insert(0, label((english, "en"), (french[english], "fr")))
ET.indent(written)
ET.ElementTree(written).write("pets-cdi.xml", encoding="utf-8", xml_declaration=True)
print(
    sum(1 for language in written.iter(f"{{{CDI}}}language") if language.text == "fr")
)  # -> 4

    The new label goes first in each category, where the schema puts displayLabel, before identifier. Validate the file again to check.

  5. (O5) Print the DDI-Lifecycle URN of the PetKind variable in the tables, then the three parts DDI-CDI writes for the same variable in pets-cdi.xml. What would make the two point to the same thing?

    Answer 
    pet_kind = tables.get("variables", "PetKind")
print(pet_kind.to_reference().urn)
# -> urn:ddi:example.org:e96e0842-d74e-5893-a7ba-b3c3fabda24d:1
written = ET.parse("pets-cdi.xml").getroot()
N = {"cdi": CDI}
for variable in written.iterfind("cdi:InstanceVariable", N):
    if variable.findtext("cdi:name/cdi:name", namespaces=N) == "PetKind":
        parts = variable.find("cdi:identifier/cdi:ddiIdentifier", N)
        print([part.text for part in parts])
# -> ['variable-PetKind', 'example.org', '1']

    Both have an agency, an identifier and a version. The DDI-CDI file uses identifiers of its own, such as variable-PetKind. To make the two descriptions of the variable the same object, give DDI-CDI the DDI-Lifecycle identifier: pass pet_kind.identifier and pet_kind.version to identifier() instead.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Question 1 (O1): What does DDI-CDI describe that DDI-Lifecycle does not?

A. Questionnaires and their routing.

B. The data themselves, in wide, long, multidimensional or key-value structures, and the processes that produced them, across domains.

C. Code lists.

D. Study titles.

Answer

B. Questionnaires are DDI-Lifecycle's strength; both have code lists. DDI-CDI describes data in any shape, from any domain, down to a single value.

Question 2 (O2): A variable has the codes 1 Dog, 2 Cat and 9 Don't know. How does DDI-CDI hold them?

A. One code list, with 9 marked as missing.

B. A substantive value domain with a code list of 1 and 2, and a sentinel value domain with a code list of 9.

C. Three instance variables.

D. In the data structure.

Answer

B. DDI-CDI separates the answers from the values that stand for something else. DDI-Lifecycle does it with one code list and the isMissing flag of a category.

Question 3 (O3): In a wide data structure, what does the household identifier column get?

A. A measure component.

B. An identifier component, defined by the identifier's variable.

C. A variable value component.

D. Nothing: identifiers are not described.

Answer

B. Identifier components tell the rows apart; measure components hold what was observed.

Question 4 (O4): xmlschema.XMLSchema says DDICDIModels is not an element of the schema. Why?

A. The file has the wrong namespace.

B. The DDI-CDI schema needs an XML Schema 1.1 processor; the 1.0 validator skips it, so use xmlschema.XMLSchema11.

C. The schema file is corrupted.

D. DDICDIModels must be the last element.

Answer

B. The schema declares vc:minVersion="1.1". An XML Schema 1.0 processor honours that by ignoring the schema's content.

Question 5 (O5): What does a DDI-CDI link hold?

A. The other object, copied in full.

B. The other object's identifier (data identifier, registration authority and version) and its class in validType.

C. A file path.

D. A URN only.

Answer

B. ddiReference gives the same three parts as a DDI-Lifecycle URN, and validType says which class to expect.

items.title: Check yourself
items.text:
• I can say what DDI-CDI describes, and when to use it next to DDI-Lifecycle and DDI-Codebook. (O1)
  • I can map a coded variable with missing values onto an instance variable, two value domains and their code lists. (O2)
  • I can describe a data file as a wide data structure, and name the components a long one would use. (O3)
  • I can write DDI-CDI XML from a ddi-l study and validate it with xmlschema.XMLSchema11. (O4)
  • I can explain a DDI-CDI identifier and link, and how they compare with a DDI-Lifecycle URN. (O5)

Instructor notes

  • Start with the table of section 1 and a real case from the room: a project that combines files of different shapes. DDI-CDI makes sense once learners have felt that problem.
  • The split between substantive and sentinel values (section 3) is the idea learners keep. Ask which values of a familiar variable are sentinels before showing the code.
  • Download the schema before the session if the room's network is slow: it is about 1 MB.
  • The file is long for three variables. That is the point of the exercise on identifiers: in practice a program writes DDI-CDI, as it does here, and nobody types it.

See also: Module 20: From DDI-Codebook to DDI-Lifecycle, built for reuse | Work with other tools | DDI-CDI at the DDI Alliance

items.title: Schema conversion benchmark
items.text: This page outlines a baseline benchmark for converting schema definitions into ddi-l objects. Use it to validate performance changes and to keep regression testing repeatable.

items.title: Benchmark objective
items.text:
• Measure the time and memory required to parse, validate, and convert schema sources.
  • Capture the impact of caching, streaming, and batching options.

items.title: Dataset
items.text:
• Include a representative DDI schema bundle and a large sample XML instance.
  • Note the file sizes and any simplifications used for the benchmark run.

items.title: Procedure
items.text:
1. Warm up the environment by running a no-op command to load dependencies.
  2. Execute the conversion command against the benchmark dataset.
  3. Repeat runs at least three times and record the median.
  4. Compare results when toggling key options (e.g., caching, parallelism, schema reuse).

items.title: Metrics to collect
items.text:
• Wall-clock duration for the full conversion pipeline.
  • Peak memory usage and steady-state footprint.
  • Number of warnings or validation errors encountered.

items.title: Reporting template
items.text:
Use the following skeleton to log results:

### Environment
- Hardware:
- Python:
- Dependencies:

### Dataset
- Schema bundle:
- Instance file:

### Results
- Median runtime:
- Peak memory:
- Notes:

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Share findings in the performance playbook and update recommendations.
  • Extend the benchmark to cover new schema features as they are added.

  • API reference

  • Models reference

  • Lint rules

  • Namespace catalog

  • Schema coverage

    How much of DDI Lifecycle 3.3 ddi-l supports, and at which level.

The cheat sheet puts the most used calls on one page, and the release notes say what changed in each version.

items.title: Command-line automation playbook
items.text:
This playbook chains the ddi CLI commands into repeatable automation tasks that you can add to CI/CD pipelines. The exercises cover exit codes, logging and keeping the output files, so that a failed run tells you what to fix.

Before you start

Install ddi-l with pip install ddi-l. The commands below use sample files that ship with the package. Run this once in Python to copy them into an examples/ folder in your working directory:

import shutil
from importlib.resources import files
from pathlib import Path

Path("examples").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ("Quality_of_Life.xml", "example_instance.xml", "example_fragment.xml"):
    shutil.copy(files("ddi_l.examples") / name, "examples")

items.title: 1. Validate and capture JSON reports
items.text:
The examples use the bundled sample examples/Quality_of_Life.xml; replace it with your own file before running the commands if needed.

  1. Create the reports directory with mkdir -p reports so that redirecting output succeeds even when the workspace starts empty.
  2. Run ddi validate --format json examples/Quality_of_Life.xml > reports/validation.json.
  3. Inspect the exit status: a zero status indicates success, while 1 means validation failed. The redirected output is a JSON array of issues, empty when the document is valid.
  4. Capture the output in your CI pipeline so that successful runs record an empty array and failing runs persist the JSON payload for further analysis.

items.title: 2. Convert XML to JSON for downstream systems
items.text:
1. Create an output directory (for example build/artifacts).
  2. Execute ddi to-json examples/Quality_of_Life.xml --indent 2 > build/artifacts/quality_of_life.json.
  3. Store the generated JSON in your build artefacts so analytics systems can ingest structured data without parsing XML.

items.title: 3. Round-trip conversions as a regression guard
items.text:
1. Create the round-trip output directory with mkdir -p build/roundtrip before running conversions; you only need to create it once per workspace.
  2. Run ddi roundtrip examples/Quality_of_Life.xml --output build/roundtrip/Quality_of_Life.xml to read the document and write it back; what it did not change is written as read.
  3. Pass flags such as --validate, --no-pretty-print, or --no-declaration when you need schema checks or to adjust the emitted XML.
  4. Diff the regenerated XML against the original to ensure the converter is stable. Include this diff as part of your pull request checks.

items.title: 4. Bundle the workflow into a script
items.text:
1. Create scripts/validate.sh with the following content. It defaults to the examples/Quality_of_Life.xml sample you copied above; pass another file as the first argument:

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

INPUT=${1:-examples/Quality_of_Life.xml}
REPORT_DIR=${2:-reports}

mkdir -p "$REPORT_DIR" build/artifacts build/roundtrip

ddi validate "$INPUT" > "$REPORT_DIR"/validation.json
ddi to-json "$INPUT" --indent 2 \
  > build/artifacts/$(basename "$INPUT" .xml).json
ROUNDTRIP_OUTPUT="build/roundtrip/$(basename "$INPUT")"
ddi roundtrip "$INPUT" --output "$ROUNDTRIP_OUTPUT"

  2. Mark the script as executable (chmod +x scripts/validate.sh).

  3. Call the script from your CI configuration and rely on the non-zero exit code to fail the pipeline when validation or conversion encounters an error.

items.title: 5. Surface findings in CI dashboards
items.text:
• Review and redact reports/validation.json before uploading it and build/artifacts as build artefacts so stakeholders can review them without digging into logs.
  • Parse the JSON report (after confirming any sensitive content is removed) to comment on pull requests or annotate commits when violations occur.
  • Schedule the script to run nightly against canonical instances to detect drift even when no code changes are in flight, but ensure the published output is redacted appropriately.

Caution

Scrub identifiers or restrict access to the generated artefacts whenever they contain confidential data before sharing them on dashboards or other collaborative platforms.

items.title: Build tools and applications with ddi-l
items.text:
This guide is for developers who want to use ddi-l as a foundation for their own products: dashboards, web services, CLI utilities, or data pipelines.

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11+ with ddi-l installed.
  • Familiarity with the user guide and the models reference.

items.title: Read and query documents
items.text:
import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.open_ddi("study.xml")

# Access typed collections
for q in doc.questions:
    print(q.identifier)

for v in doc.variables:
    print(v.identifier)

# Find by identifier
item = doc.find("some-id")

# Query any registered type
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Category

categories = doc.items(Category)

items.title: Create documents programmatically
items.text:
doc = ddi.new_study(title="Generated Survey", agency="app.org")

questions = ["Age", "Gender", "Income"]
for text in questions:
    q = doc.add_question(text=f"What is your {text.lower()}?")
    doc.add_variable(name=text, question=q)

doc.save("generated-survey.xml")

items.title: Integrate validation
items.text:
doc = ddi.open_ddi("input.xml", validate=True)

issues = doc.validate()
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        report_to_dashboard(issue.severity, issue.message)

items.title: Work with the advanced model layer
items.text:
For fine-grained control, use the model classes directly:

from ddi_l.document import DDIDocument
from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable

instance = DDIDocument.from_xml("study.xml")

# Access raw XML
root = instance.root

# Build an index for cross-reference resolution
index = instance.build_index()

items.title: CLI integration
items.text:
Wrap the ddi CLI in your automation:

ddi validate *.xml                     # Batch validation
ddi to-json study.xml --indent 2       # Export for web APIs
ddi roundtrip input.xml --output output.xml --layout default  # Normalize formatting

items.title: Architecture tips
items.text:
• Use ddi.new_study() and ddi.open_ddi() for most workflows. Drop to DDIDocument only when you need the raw XML tree.
  • The add_item() / items() generic methods cover all 30 DDI item types, so you can write type-agnostic code.
  • All model classes preserve unknown XML in other_elements, so round-trips are lossless even for content the library does not model.

items.title: Fragment reuse lab
items.text:
This lab expands on the fragment rebuild script in ddi_l.examples to teach how to package reusable fragments, distribute them to other teams, and reuse them in new DDI instances.

Before you start

Install ddi-l with pip install ddi-l. The steps below use sample files that ship with the package. Run this once in Python to copy them into an examples/ folder in your working directory:

import shutil
from importlib.resources import files
from pathlib import Path

Path("examples").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ("Quality_of_Life.xml", "example_instance.xml", "example_fragment.xml"):
    shutil.copy(files("ddi_l.examples") / name, "examples")

items.title: 1. Rebuild the example fragment bundle
items.text:
1. Regenerate the sample bundle into your examples/ folder:

    python -m ddi_l.examples.build_and_validate --refresh --refresh-fragment \
  --output examples/example_instance.xml \
  --fragment-output examples/example_fragment.xml

    The script rewrites both files and prints a confirmation that both payloads validate. Without --output and --fragment-output it writes both files into the current folder. 2. Inspect the refreshed instance and fragment XML outputs to see how the maintainables are packaged and how the validation messages describe the rebuild. 3. Re-run the command with --fragment-output if you want the fragment to be written to another location (for example --fragment-output fragments/catalog/example_fragment.xml) so teams know where to pick up the reusable artefact.

items.title: 2. Publish fragments for team consumption
items.text:
Compliance review before distribution

De-identify fragment payloads, strip production URNs, and align with your organisation's data-handling rules before sharing archives with other teams. Follow the redaction guidance in the CLI automation playbook to keep tutorials consistent.

  1. Copy the generated fragments into a shared location (for example fragments/catalog).
  2. Create a README that documents the fragment purpose, maintainable identifiers, and versioning scheme.
  3. Optionally zip the fragments and validation report together so downstream consumers have a single artefact to download.

items.title: 3. Consume fragments in a new project
items.text:
1. Start a new Python script and load both the target document and fragment:

    from ddi_l import MaintainableBase
from ddi_l.document import DDIDocument, DDIFragment

document = DDIDocument.from_xml("instances/source.ddi.xml")
fragment = DDIFragment.from_xml("fragments/catalog/study-fragment.xml")

  2. Iterate over :meth:ddi_l.document.DDIFragment.iter_fragment_payloads and attach each maintainable to the document explicitly:

    for payload in fragment.iter_fragment_payloads():
    maintainable_cls = MaintainableBase.for_tag(payload.tag)
    if maintainable_cls is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported payload: {payload.tag}")
    document.add_maintainable(maintainable_cls.from_xml(payload))

  3. Serialise the enriched instance and run ddi validate to confirm the fragments integrate cleanly.

items.title: 4. Maintain fragment provenance
items.text:
• Track fragment versions in your source control system and tag releases so consuming teams can pin to specific builds.
  • Include a changelog with each fragment release that notes schema versions and lint expectations.
  • Automate fragment rebuilds in CI to ensure new changes remain compatible with the canonical instance.

items.title: Schema troubleshooting clinic
items.text:
Practice diagnosing schema errors with the command line and the Python API. Each exercise starts from a deliberately broken file: you read the error output, then fix the file.

Before you start

Install ddi-l with pip install ddi-l. The steps below use sample files that ship with the package. Run this once in Python to copy them into an examples/ folder in your working directory:

import shutil
from importlib.resources import files
from pathlib import Path

Path("examples").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ("Quality_of_Life.xml", "example_instance.xml", "example_fragment.xml"):
    shutil.copy(files("ddi_l.examples") / name, "examples")

items.title: 1. Trigger a failing validation
items.text:
1. Run mkdir -p clinic to create a workspace that keeps the broken instance separate from the source samples.
  2. Copy examples/Quality_of_Life.xml to clinic/broken-instance.xml.
  3. Remove a required attribute (for example the version on a StudyUnit) using your editor.
  4. Run ddi validate clinic/broken-instance.xml to list each issue with its message, line and XPath. Add --format json for a JSON array instead.
  5. Note the XPath and message for the failing node.

items.title: 2. Reproduce the error programmatically
items.text:
1. Launch a Python session and validate the same file with the schema loader. Passing raise_error=False collects the full error list instead of raising on the first failure:

    from ddi_l.schema_loader import validate

errors = validate("clinic/broken-instance.xml", raise_error=False)
for error in errors:
    print("message:", error.message)
    print("xpath:", error.xpath)
    print("line:", error.line)
    print("column:", error.column)

  2. Compare the output to the CLI JSON structure. Both surfaces expose the same error metadata so you can choose whichever fits your tooling.

items.title: 3. Connect findings to lint rules
items.text:
1. Open docs/validation.md and identify which lint rules would catch similar mistakes (for example, missing agency identifiers).
  2. Update your lint profile to include those rules by calling configure_lint() in a Python session or editing your team profile file.

  3. Still in Python, execute run_profile against the broken instance to confirm the rule set surfaces the issue before the schema fails:

    from ddi_l.io import read
from ddi_l.lint import DDI_PROFILE_DEFAULT, configure_lint, run_profile

configure_lint()  # optionally tighten agencies, citation rules, etc.
document = read("clinic/broken-instance.xml")
result = run_profile(document, DDI_PROFILE_DEFAULT)
for finding in result.lint_findings:
    print(finding.rule_id, finding.message)

items.title: 4. Establish a remediation checklist
items.text:
• Ensure the failing node's namespace prefix is registered so schema lookups can resolve the element correctly.
  • Restore required attributes and run ddi validate until the command reports Document is valid..
  • Capture representative examples of the error and fix in your team's runbook so future incidents can be triaged faster.

items.title: From XML to objects
items.text: This tutorial shows how to move between raw DDI XML and the ddi-l Python objects. It covers opening XML files, exploring their contents, and working with the model layer for fine-grained control.

items.title: 1. Open a DDI file with the simple API
items.text:
The easiest way to work with existing DDI XML is ddi.open_ddi():

import ddi_l as ddi

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml")

print(f"Questions: {len(doc.questions)}")
print(f"Variables: {len(doc.variables)}")
print(f"Concepts: {len(doc.concepts)}")

for v in doc.variables:
    print(f"  Variable: {v.identifier}")

The Document object gives you access to all items through typed properties and the generic items() method.

items.title: 2. Open with the advanced layer
items.text:
For full control, use DDIDocument.from_xml():

from ddi_l.document import DDIDocument

instance = DDIDocument.from_xml("my-study.xml", validate=True)
print(instance.get_identification())

DDIDocument gives you access to the raw XML tree and all the model objects parsed from it.

items.title: 3. Work with model objects
items.text:
Model objects are thin dataclasses. Each one supports from_xml() and to_xml():

from ddi_l.models.logicalproduct import Variable

# Get a variable from the document
var = doc.variables[0]
print(var.agency, var.identifier, var.version)

# Convert to XML element
xml_element = var.to_xml()

items.title: 4. Round-trip XML
items.text:
You can parse, modify, and re-serialize without losing content:

doc = ddi.open_ddi("my-study.xml")
doc.add_question(text="New question")
doc.save("my-study-updated.xml")

Unknown XML elements are preserved in the other_elements list, so round-tripping does not drop content the library does not model.

items.title: 5. CLI round-trip
items.text:
The CLI also supports round-tripping:

ddi roundtrip my-study.xml --output my-study-roundtrip.xml --validate
